44006.e: The Palace of Versailles is near Paris. It has a famous Hall of Mirrors and a huge park.
44006.m: Louis XIV had the Palace of Versailles built.

44007.q: Which animal is a well-known symbol of France?
44007.e: The Gallic cockerel is an old symbol of France. You often see it on sports teams.
44007.m: The cockerel is a symbol of France.

44008.q: Which soft cheese comes from France?
44008.e: Camembert comes from Normandy in the north of France. It is soft inside and has a white rind.
44008.m: Camembert is a cheese from France.

44009.q: Which German city has the biggest port in the country?
44009.e: Hamburg lies on the river Elbe, not far from the North Sea. Huge container ships dock there.
44009.m: Hamburg has the biggest port in Germany.

44010.q: In which German city on the Rhine is there a famous cathedral with two tall towers?
44010.e: Cologne Cathedral is over 150 metres high. People worked on building it for over 600 years.
44010.m: Cologne Cathedral stands on the Rhine.

44011.q: In which German city does the Oktoberfest take place every year?
44011.e: The Oktoberfest in Munich is the biggest folk festival in the world. It already starts in September.
44011.m: The Oktoberfest takes place in Munich.

44012.q: Which two seas does Germany border?
a: The North Sea and the Baltic Sea
The Mediterranean and the North Sea
The Baltic Sea and the Mediterranean
The Black Sea and the Baltic Sea
44012.e: In the north Germany lies on the North Sea and the Baltic Sea. There are lots of islands and beaches there.
44012.m: Germany lies on the North Sea and the Baltic Sea.

44013.q: Which fairy-tale castle stands in Bavaria?
44013.e: King Ludwig II had Neuschwanstein Castle built. It looks like a castle from a fairy tale.
44013.m: Neuschwanstein is a fairy-tale castle in Bavaria.

44014.q: How many neighbouring countries does Germany have?
44014.e: Germany borders nine countries, for example Switzerland, France, Poland and Denmark.

44015.q: Which large island in the Mediterranean belongs to Italy?
44015.e: Sardinia lies west of the Italian mainland and belongs to Italy. Corsica belongs to France.

44016.q: Which big Italian city lies not far from Ticino and is known for fashion?
44016.e: Milan is in Lombardy, about an hour's drive from Lugano. The city is famous for fashion and its cathedral.
44016.m: Milan is a big fashion city near Switzerland.

44017.q: What is the longest river in Italy called?
44017.e: The Po flows through northern Italy to the Adriatic Sea. It is the longest river in the country.
44017.m: The Po is the longest river in Italy.

44018.q: Which neighbouring country lies to the south of Switzerland?
44018.e: South of the Alps, Valais, Ticino and the Grisons border Italy.
44018.m: Italy lies to the south of Switzerland.

44019.q: Which breaded meat dish is typical of Austria?
44019.e: Wiener Schnitzel is a thin, breaded veal escalope. It is a national dish of Austria.
44019.m: Wiener Schnitzel is a typical dish from Austria.

44020.e: Austria lies in the middle of Europe and has no coast. Just like Switzerland, it is a landlocked country.

44021.q: Which city in Tyrol has hosted the Winter Olympics twice?
44021.e: Innsbruck hosted the Winter Olympics in 1964 and 1976. The city lies right in the middle of the Alps.
44021.m: Innsbruck has hosted the Winter Olympics twice.

44022.q: Which river flows from the Engadine to Austria?
44022.e: The Inn rises in the Engadine in the Grisons. It flows through Tyrol and later joins the Danube.
44022.m: The Inn flows from the Engadine to Austria.

44024.q: What has Liechtenstein not had since 1868?
44024.e: Liechtenstein abolished its army in 1868. Since then the country has had no soldiers.

44025.q: What is the well-known ski resort in Liechtenstein called?
44025.e: Malbun lies in the mountains of the municipality of Triesenberg. It is the only big ski resort in Liechtenstein.

44026.q: What is Liechtenstein famous for among collectors?
44026.e: For over 100 years Liechtenstein has issued its own beautifully designed stamps. There is even a postal museum in Vaduz.
44026.m: Liechtenstein is known for its stamps.

44027.e: Liechtenstein is too small for its own airport. People who want to fly usually travel to Zurich.
44027.m: Liechtenstein has no airport of its own.

44028.q: Which border town in Ticino lies at the very south of Switzerland?
44028.e: Chiasso lies right on the border with Italy. The southernmost point of Switzerland is near Chiasso.
44028.m: Chiasso lies at the very south of Switzerland.

44029.q: Where does the border run in Lake Geneva?
a: Through the middle of the lake
44029.e: The border between Switzerland and France runs through the water in the middle of Lake Geneva.
44029.m: The border runs through the middle of Lake Geneva.

44030.q: Which pass takes you from Valais straight to Italy?
44030.e: The Great St Bernard links Valais with the Aosta Valley in Italy. The border is at the top of the pass.
44030.m: You can get to Italy over the Great St Bernard.

44031.q: What do you call a piece of a country that is completely surrounded by another country?
44031.e: An exclave belongs to one country but lies completely within the territory of another. One example is Büsingen.
44031.m: An exclave is surrounded by a foreign country.

44032.q: What were the officials called who guarded Switzerland's open border away from the crossings?
44032.e: Border guards also checked the border away from the crossing points. Today they are part of Swiss customs.
44032.m: Border guards watched over the border.

44033.q: Which river forms part of the border with France in the Jura?
44033.e: The Doubs flows through the Jura. Over a long stretch it separates Switzerland from France.
44033.m: The Doubs forms the border with France in the Jura.

44034.q: What is it called when people from Switzerland go shopping more cheaply in a nearby country?
44034.e: Many people cross the border to shop because lots of things are cheaper there. This is called shopping tourism.
44034.m: Shopping abroad is called shopping tourism.

44035.q: Since 2025, up to what value per person per day can you bring purchases into Switzerland without paying VAT?
44035.e: Since 1 January 2025 the duty-free allowance has been 150 francs per person per day. Before that it was 300 francs.
44035.m: The duty-free allowance is 150 francs per person per day.

44036.q: Why are you not allowed to bring ivory souvenirs into Switzerland?
44036.e: Ivory comes from elephants' tusks. To protect these animals, trading in ivory is forbidden.
44036.m: Ivory may not be imported because elephants are protected.

44037.q: What is the money called that you have to pay for some goods at the border?
44037.e: If you buy a lot abroad, you sometimes have to pay customs duty at the border. This money goes to the state.
44037.m: For some goods you pay customs duty at the border.

44038.q: In which city is the Swiss embassy in Germany?
44038.e: Embassies are usually in the capital. That is why the Swiss embassy in Germany is in Berlin, near the Federal Chancellery.
44038.m: The Swiss embassy in Germany is in Berlin.

44039.q: Which country does the ground under a foreign embassy in Bern belong to?
44039.e: The ground of an embassy remains part of the host country. However, the embassy is specially protected.
44039.m: Even under an embassy, the ground is Swiss territory.

44040.q: Which letters are on diplomats' number plates in Switzerland?
44040.e: CD stands for “Corps Diplomatique”. This is how you recognise cars belonging to embassies and diplomats.
44040.m: Diplomats' cars have the letters CD.

44041.q: Which holiday do Swiss embassies abroad celebrate with guests?
44041.e: 1 August is the Swiss National Day. Many Swiss embassies then invite guests to a celebration.

44042.q: Since 1980, which country has Switzerland represented as a protecting power in Iran?
44042.e: Since 1980 the USA and Iran have had no embassies in each other's countries. That is why Switzerland represents the USA in Iran.
44042.m: Switzerland represents the USA in Iran.

44044.q: In which city is the Swiss embassy in Italy?
44044.e: Embassies are usually in a country's capital. That is why the Swiss embassy in Italy is in Rome.
44044.m: The Swiss embassy in Italy is in Rome.

44045.q: How many embassies does a country usually have in another country?
44045.e: A country usually has only one embassy in another country. Sometimes there are also consulates in other cities.
44045.m: A country usually has just one embassy in each country.

44046.q: Which capital of a country neighbouring Switzerland has the most inhabitants?
44046.e: About 3.7 million people live in Berlin (as of 2024). That is more than in any other capital of a neighbouring country.
44046.m: Berlin is the biggest capital among the neighbouring countries.

44047.q: In which capital is the famous Ferris wheel in the Prater?
44047.e: The Ferris wheel in Vienna's Prater was built in 1897. It is one of the city's landmarks.
44047.m: The Ferris wheel in the Prater is in Vienna.

44048.e: The Spree flows right through Berlin, past the Reichstag building.

44049.q: Which capital is also a federal state of Austria in its own right?
44049.e: Vienna is a city and at the same time one of Austria's federal states.
44049.m: Vienna is both a city and a federal state.

44050.q: Which famous church in Paris burned in 2019 and reopened in 2024?
44050.e: In April 2019 the roof of Notre-Dame Cathedral burned. After being rebuilt, it reopened in December 2024.
44050.m: Notre-Dame in Paris was rebuilt after the fire.

44051.q: Which animal is on the coat of arms of Berlin, just like Bern?
44051.e: Berlin's coat of arms has a black bear on it. The city of Bern also has a bear on its coat of arms.
44051.m: Berlin and Bern both have a bear on their coats of arms.

44052.q: What is the Italian word for ice cream?
44052.e: Ice cream is “gelato” in Italian. In Italy there are lots of gelaterias.
44052.m: Ice cream is gelato in Italian.

44054.q: What do you say in French when saying goodbye?
44054.e: “Au revoir” means “goodbye”. “Merci” means “thank you” and “S'il vous plaît” means “please”.
44054.m: To say goodbye in French you say “Au revoir”.

44055.q: Which train do many cross-border commuters from France take to Geneva?
44055.e: The Léman Express has run between Geneva and France since 2019. It links places such as Annemasse with the city of Geneva.
44055.m: The Léman Express links Geneva with France.

44056.q: Why do many people from neighbouring countries work in Switzerland?
44056.e: In Switzerland people usually earn more money than in the neighbouring countries. That is why many cross the border to work.
44056.m: Many cross-border commuters come because of the higher wages.

44057.q: What are cross-border commuters called in French?
44057.e: “Frontière” means “border”. That is why cross-border commuters are called “frontaliers” in French.
44057.m: Cross-border commuters are called frontaliers in French.

44058.q: Which country do most cross-border commuters working in Schaffhausen come from?
44058.e: The canton of Schaffhausen is almost completely surrounded by German territory. That is why its cross-border commuters come mainly from Germany.
44058.m: Many cross-border commuters from Germany work in Schaffhausen.

44059.q: Which two neighbouring countries does the city of Basel border?
44059.e: Basel lies on the Rhine where three countries meet. Many cross-border commuters from France and Germany work in Basel.

44060.q: Why do many cross-border commuters live abroad rather than in Geneva?
44060.e: In Geneva flats are very expensive and hard to find. In nearby France housing is usually cheaper.
44060.m: Many cross-border commuters live abroad because housing is cheaper there.

44061.q: Are cross-border commuters counted as part of Switzerland's population?
44061.e: Cross-border commuters work in Switzerland but live abroad. That is why they are not counted in Switzerland's resident population.
44061.m: Cross-border commuters are not part of Switzerland's resident population.

44062.q: Which language do cross-border commuters from France usually speak at work in Geneva?
44062.e: French is the official language in Geneva. So cross-border commuters from France can speak their own language at work.
44062.m: In Geneva people mostly work in French.

44063.q: What is the smaller, western part of Lake Constance called?
44063.e: Lake Constance is made up of the large Obersee and the smaller Untersee. Steckborn, for example, lies on the Untersee.
44063.m: The smaller part of Lake Constance is called the Untersee.

44064.q: Which German town on Lake Constance has its old town on an island?
44064.e: Lindau's old town lies on an island in Lake Constance. A causeway and a bridge link it to the mainland.
44064.m: Lindau has an old town on an island.

44065.q: Which island in Lake Constance is known for vegetables and old monasteries?
44065.e: Lots of vegetables are grown on the island of Reichenau. Its old churches are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
44065.m: Reichenau is the vegetable island in Lake Constance.

44066.q: Which old houses can you visit at Unteruhldingen on Lake Constance?
44066.e: At Unteruhldingen there are rebuilt houses standing on stilts in the water. This is how people lived by the lake thousands of years ago.
44066.m: You can visit pile dwellings on Lake Constance.

44067.q: Why is the water of Lake Constance important for millions of people?
44067.e: Lots of drinking water is taken from Lake Constance. It flows through long pipes far into southern Germany, for example to Stuttgart.
44067.m: Lake Constance supplies drinking water for millions of people.

44069.q: Which fish is caught especially often in Lake Constance?
44069.e: Whitefish is the most important food fish in Lake Constance. It is often served fried.
44069.m: In Lake Constance people mainly catch whitefish.

44070.q: According to the Federal Constitution, what applies to all authorities?
a: They may only act if the law allows it
They may do what they like
They must have every decision approved by the people
They must always obey the President of the Confederation
44070.e: Article 5 says that the law is the basis and the limit of state action. So authorities always need a rule that allows them to act.
44070.m: The state may only act on the basis of the law.

44072.q: Which legal text is at the very top of the order of law in Switzerland?
a: An ordinance of the Federal Council
44072.e: The Federal Constitution is the highest law of the country. Federal acts and ordinances must be compatible with it.
44072.m: The Federal Constitution is the highest law in Switzerland.

44073.q: Which four national languages does the Federal Constitution name?
44073.e: Article 4 of the Federal Constitution names German, French, Italian and Romansh as national languages.

44074.q: What is the Federal Constitution called in French?
44074.e: The Federal Constitution is published with equal status in the official languages. In French it is called “Constitution fédérale”, in Italian “Costituzione federale”.
44074.m: In French the Federal Constitution is called “Constitution fédérale”.

44075.q: According to Article 5 of the Federal Constitution, what must the federal government and the cantons respect besides national law?
44075.e: Article 5 paragraph 4 says: “The Confederation and the cantons shall respect international law.” This includes international treaties, for example.
44075.m: The federal government and the cantons must respect international law.

44076.q: The state must act “proportionately”. What does that mean?
a: It may not intervene more strictly than necessary
It must always spend the same amount of money
It may only act once a year
44076.e: A measure must be suitable and may not restrict more than necessary. This is stated in Article 5 of the Federal Constitution.
44076.m: Proportionate means no stricter than necessary.

44078.q: What is the majority of the cantons in a vote on the constitution called?
44078.e: In votes on the constitution, what counts besides the people is in how many cantons a majority agrees. This is called the majority of the cantons.
44078.m: In votes on the constitution, the majority of the cantons counts as well as the people.

44079.q: Which fundamental right protects the freedom of research and teaching?
44079.e: Article 20 of the Federal Constitution guarantees the freedom of academic teaching and research.
44079.m: Academic freedom protects research and teaching.

44080.q: Which fundamental right protects painters, musicians and writers in their work?
44080.e: Article 21 says: “Freedom of artistic expression is guaranteed.”

44081.q: Which treatment does the Federal Constitution expressly ban in the article on personal freedom?
44081.e: Article 10 bans torture and any other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment. Prison sentences and fines, on the other hand, are allowed if a court imposes them.

44082.q: Who is first and foremost bound by fundamental rights and must respect them?
44082.e: Fundamental rights protect the individual against the state. Anyone carrying out state tasks is bound by them (Article 35).
44082.m: Fundamental rights protect people from abuses by the state.

44083.q: May fundamental rights be restricted in Switzerland?
a: Yes, but only under strict conditions
44083.e: Fundamental rights may only be restricted if a law allows it, there is a public interest and the restriction is proportionate. The core of a fundamental right always remains protected.
44083.m: Fundamental rights may only be restricted under strict conditions.

44084.q: Which fundamental right protects the right to use your own language?
44084.e: Article 18 of the Federal Constitution guarantees freedom of language. In dealings with the authorities, however, the official languages apply.
44084.m: Freedom of language protects the use of your own language.

44085.q: Which fundamental right guarantees help and care for people in need?
a: Right to assistance when in need
44085.e: Article 12 gives people in need the right to help and to the means that are essential for a life in human dignity.
44085.m: Anyone in need has the right to help.

44086.q: According to the Federal Constitution, what are court hearings and the announcement of judgements in principle?
44086.e: Article 30 paragraph 3 states that court hearings and the announcement of judgements are public. The law may provide for exceptions.
44086.m: Court hearings in Switzerland are public in principle.

44087.q: According to Article 31, what must an arrested person be told immediately?
a: The reasons for the arrest and their rights
The weather for the next day
44087.e: Anyone who is arrested must be told immediately, in a language they understand, the reasons and their rights.
44087.m: Arrested people must immediately learn the reasons and their rights.

44088.q: Which fundamental right protects the right to marry and start a family?
a: Right to marry and to have a family
44088.e: Article 14 of the Federal Constitution guarantees the right to marry and to have a family.
44088.m: The right to marry and to have a family is a fundamental right.

44089.q: Because of freedom of expression, does a private newspaper have to print every reader's letter?
a: No, freedom of expression protects against the state
44089.e: Freedom of expression forbids the state from suppressing opinions. But a private newspaper may choose for itself what it publishes.
44089.m: Freedom of expression is aimed first and foremost at the state.

44090.q: Which fundamental right allows you to inform yourself freely from generally accessible sources?
44090.e: Article 16 paragraph 3 protects the right to receive information freely and to gather it from generally accessible sources.
44090.m: Freedom of information allows you to inform yourself freely.

44091.q: Where can you turn if you think a radio or television programme breaks the law?
a: Independent Complaints Authority for Radio and Television
44091.e: The Independent Complaints Authority for Radio and Television (UBI) examines complaints about programmes. Before that you have to contact an ombudsman's office.
44091.m: Complaints about radio and TV programmes are examined by the UBI.

44092.q: What is it called when someone spreads defamatory claims about a person without knowing whether they are true?
44092.e: Defamation is a criminal offence. Unlike in malicious defamation, the offender does not know for certain that the claim is false.
44092.m: Even spreading unchecked claims that damage someone's honour can be a crime.

44093.q: Which statements are a criminal offence in Switzerland despite freedom of expression?
a: Calls to hatred because of religion or origin
An opinion different from the teacher's
44093.e: The criminal provision against discrimination and incitement to hatred (Article 261bis of the Criminal Code) sets limits on freedom of expression. Criticism of the authorities, on the other hand, is allowed.
44093.m: Freedom of expression ends where people call for hatred against groups.

44094.q: What is it called when someone knowingly spreads untrue things about a person to damage their reputation?
44094.e: Malicious defamation is an attack on someone's honour and a criminal offence. Freedom of expression does not protect deliberately false claims that harm others.
44094.m: Anyone who knowingly spreads lies about others commits malicious defamation.

44095.q: Besides incitement to hatred, which statement does the anti-racism criminal provision also punish?
44095.e: Article 261bis of the Criminal Code also punishes anyone who publicly denies or grossly trivialises a genocide or other crimes against humanity.
44095.m: Publicly denying a genocide is a criminal offence in Switzerland.

44096.q: What is the criminal provision called that bans calls to hatred because of origin or religion?
44096.e: The anti-racism criminal provision is in Article 261bis of the Criminal Code. The people accepted it in 1994.
44096.m: The anti-racism criminal provision protects against hatred and discrimination.

44097.q: What is a church called that is officially recognised under public law by a canton?
44097.e: In most cantons the Reformed Church and the Roman Catholic Church are recognised as established cantonal churches. For example, they may levy church taxes.
44097.m: Churches recognised by the canton are called established cantonal churches.

44098.q: Which two churches are recognised as established cantonal churches in most cantons?
a: The Reformed and the Roman Catholic
44098.e: In most cantons the Reformed and the Roman Catholic churches are established cantonal churches. In some cantons the Christian Catholic Church is also recognised.
44098.m: The Reformed and Catholic churches are usually established cantonal churches.

44099.q: What does the separation of church and state mean?
a: The state does not support any church directly
44099.e: With separation of church and state, the canton does not collect church tax for the churches and does not support them directly. Geneva and Neuchâtel have this separation.
44099.m: With separation of church and state, the state does not support any church directly.

44100.q: Why must state schools be religiously neutral?
a: Because children of all religions go to them
Because religion is banned in Switzerland
Because teachers may not have a religion
Because otherwise it would be too expensive
44100.e: Children of different religions or of no religion go to state schools. That is why the school may not favour any religion. For this reason, the Federal Supreme Court ruled in 1990 that crucifixes had to be removed from classrooms.
44100.m: State schools must be religiously neutral.

44101.q: May children simply stay away from compulsory swimming lessons for religious reasons?
a: Only if they can already swim
44101.e: Courts have decided that joint swimming lessons may be compulsory. The integration of the children is an important goal.
44101.m: Mixed swimming lessons may be compulsory.

44102.q: What does freedom of religion guarantee?
a: Everyone may freely choose their religion or have none
Everyone must belong to the same religion
The state decides each family's religion
44102.e: Freedom of religion and conscience is in the Federal Constitution. Nobody may be forced to join a religion or to stay in one.
44102.m: Everyone may choose their religion freely.

44103.q: Which religious community is also officially recognised in some cantons such as Basel-Stadt, Bern and Zurich?
44103.e: Several cantons have recognised Jewish communities under public law. Recognition is a matter for the cantons.
44103.m: In some cantons, Jewish communities are also officially recognised.

44104.q: Which ban did voters accept on 7 March 2021?
a: The ban on covering the face
44104.e: The popular initiative “Yes to a ban on full facial coverings” was accepted in 2021. Since then the ban has been in Article 10a of the Federal Constitution.
44104.m: Since 2021 a ban on face coverings has been in the Federal Constitution.

44105.q: Which principle protects a person who has relied on a binding statement from an authority?
44105.e: Article 9 entitles every person to be treated by authorities in good faith. The protection of trust in official assurances is based on this.
44105.m: Authorities must act in good faith.

44106.q: According to the Federal Constitution, on what principle must taxes be assessed?
a: According to where the parents live
44106.e: Article 127 requires, among other things, taxation according to economic capacity. Those who have more pay more tax.

44107.q: According to the Federal Constitution, what is a person entitled to if they cannot afford court proceedings and their case is not hopeless?
44107.e: Article 29 paragraph 3 entitles people without means to free legal aid and, if necessary, a free legal representative. That way access to justice does not depend on money.
44107.m: Even people without money should be able to get justice in court.

44108.q: What right does a person have in proceedings before an authority decides against them?
44108.e: Article 29 paragraph 2 guarantees the parties the right to be heard. They may give their view and inspect the files before a decision is made.
44108.m: Before a decision you have the right to be heard.

44109.q: Which law puts equality between women and men in working life into practice?
44109.e: The Gender Equality Act of 1996 bans discrimination in working life, for example in hiring or pay.
44109.m: The Gender Equality Act protects against disadvantage at work.

44110.q: Which federal law is meant to remove disadvantages for people with disabilities?
44110.e: The Disability Discrimination Act came into force in 2004. For example, it requires barrier-free access to public transport.
44110.m: The Disability Discrimination Act protects people with disabilities.

44111.q: Which fundamental right protects against arbitrary decisions by the authorities?
44111.e: Article 9 gives every person the right to be treated by state bodies without arbitrariness. Decisions must have objective reasons.

44112.q: What does equality before the law mean for a municipality that examines building applications?
a: Equal cases must be treated equally
44112.e: Equality before the law requires that equal things are treated equally and unequal things unequally. Personal relationships must play no part.
44112.m: Authorities must treat equal cases equally.

44113.q: Which question is in principle not allowed in a job interview because it can lead to discrimination?
44113.e: Under the Gender Equality Act, nobody may be disadvantaged because of a pregnancy. Asking about a pregnancy is therefore not allowed in principle.
44113.m: A pregnancy must play no part in hiring.

44114.q: What is it called when the police check people only because of their skin colour or appearance?
44114.e: Racial profiling means people are checked without any specific suspicion because of outward features. This goes against the ban on discrimination.
44114.m: Checks only because of skin colour are discriminatory.

44115.q: What does the ban on discrimination in the Federal Constitution forbid?
a: Disadvantaging people because of their origin or sex
44115.e: Nobody may be disadvantaged, for example, because of origin, sex, age, language, religion or a disability. This is in the Federal Constitution.
44115.m: Nobody may be disadvantaged because of origin, sex or disability.

44116.q: Who does the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities especially protect?
44116.e: The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities requires states to protect people with disabilities from disadvantage. Switzerland has signed it too.
44116.m: The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities protects people with disabilities.

44117.q: A landlady turns down a family only because of their skin colour. What is that called?
44117.e: Anyone who disadvantages people because of skin colour or origin is discriminating on racial grounds. Services offered to the public may not be refused for this reason.
44117.m: Disadvantage because of skin colour is racial discrimination.

44118.q: What is disadvantage called that is based only on a person's age?
44118.e: Age is one of the features that Article 8 paragraph 2 names expressly. Anyone who is disadvantaged only because of their age experiences age discrimination.
44118.m: Nobody may be disadvantaged only because of their age.

44119.q: Is it forbidden discrimination if a bus has ramps for wheelchairs?
a: No, it helps put disadvantaged people on an equal footing
Yes, it is against the constitution
Yes, because not all buses have ramps
44119.e: Measures that make up for disadvantages are allowed and welcome. The constitution even requires disadvantages for people with disabilities to be removed.
44119.m: Measures to balance out disadvantages are not discrimination.

44120.q: Which feature in the ban on discrimination protects, for example, people who live together without being married?
44120.e: Article 8 paragraph 2 bans discrimination because of a person's way of life. This includes, for example, unmarried couples living together or same-sex couples.
44120.m: Nobody may be discriminated against because of their way of life.

44121.q: Under the Data Protection Act, what may you ask a company?
a: What data it has about me
44121.e: Everyone has a right of access. They may ask what data a company is processing about them.
44121.m: You may ask what data a company has about you.

44122.q: What is the federal body called that supervises data protection in Switzerland?
a: Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner
44122.e: The Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC) supervises compliance with the Data Protection Act by federal bodies and private parties.
44122.m: The FDPIC watches over data protection in Switzerland.

44124.q: Which right allows you to get your own data from a provider in a common format and take it with you?
a: Right to data release and portability
44124.e: The revised Data Protection Act gives everyone the right to ask for their data in a common electronic format or to have it transferred.
44124.m: You may take your data with you from a provider.

44125.q: What is the European Union's data protection regulation called?
44125.e: The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) has applied in the EU since 25 May 2018. It also affects Swiss companies with customers in the EU.
44125.m: The GDPR is the EU's data protection law.

44126.q: May you publish a photo of a classmate on the internet without her consent?
a: No, she has a right to her own image
Yes, if the photo is funny
Yes, if you took it yourself
44126.e: Everyone has a right to their own image as part of their personal rights. In principle, recognisable photos may only be published with consent.
44126.m: You need other people's consent before publishing photos of them.

44127.q: Whose data does the Swiss Data Protection Act protect?
44127.e: Since 2023 the Data Protection Act only protects the data of people. Companies' data is no longer covered.
44127.m: The Data Protection Act protects people's data.

44128.q: What must the cantons offer for children with disabilities?
44128.e: The Federal Constitution requires the cantons to offer adequate special needs education for children with disabilities. They too have a right to education.
44128.m: Children with disabilities also have a right to schooling.

44129.q: Who is mainly responsible for schools in Switzerland?
44129.e: Article 62 of the Federal Constitution states that the cantons are responsible for the school system.
44129.m: Schools are a matter for the cantons.

44130.q: According to the Federal Constitution, who runs the Federal Institutes of Technology?
44130.e: Article 63a paragraph 1 says: “The Confederation shall operate the Federal Institutes of Technology.” The universities, on the other hand, are mostly run by the cantons.
44130.m: The ETH are run by the federal government.

44131.q: Which international agreement guarantees every child a right to education?
a: UN Convention on the Rights of the Child
44131.e: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child of 1989 contains the right to education. Switzerland ratified it in 1997.
44131.m: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child guarantees the right to education.

44132.q: According to the Federal Constitution, who makes the rules on vocational education?
44132.e: Article 63 states that the federal government makes the rules on vocational education. That is why apprenticeships are regulated in the same way throughout Switzerland.
44132.m: The federal government makes the rules for vocational education.

44133.q: Is going to primary school voluntary in Switzerland?
44133.e: According to Article 62, primary school education is compulsory and under state management or supervision.
44133.m: Going to school is compulsory in Switzerland.

44134.q: Who mainly awards grants for education in Switzerland?
44134.e: In Switzerland, grants and education loans are mainly a matter for the cantons. The federal government contributes to them.
44134.m: Grants are mainly awarded by the cantons.

44135.q: What does the right to education belong to?
44135.e: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948 says that everyone has the right to education.
44135.m: The right to education is a human right.

44136.q: What does the guarantee of ownership protect?
44136.e: The guarantee of ownership in the Federal Constitution protects property, for example a house or a plot of land. The state may only take it away under strict conditions and with compensation.
44136.m: The guarantee of ownership protects what belongs to you.

44137.q: What is a person entitled to if the state expropriates their land for a road?
a: A seat on the municipal council
44137.e: According to Article 26, expropriations and restrictions of ownership that amount to expropriation are fully compensated.
44137.m: With an expropriation, there is full compensation.

44138.q: What is it called when the state takes away property in the public interest?
44138.e: In an expropriation, someone has to give up their property, such as land, for a public project. This requires a law and compensation.
44138.m: Expropriation is the state taking away property in return for compensation.

44139.q: Which rule often restricts the guarantee of ownership when building?
44139.e: Because of spatial planning, landowners may not build everywhere. Outside the building zones, building is heavily restricted.
44139.m: Building zones limit where you may build on your land.

44140.q: Who usually officially certifies the purchase of a plot of land in Switzerland?
44140.e: A purchase of land is only valid if it is publicly certified. This is usually done by a notary.
44140.m: Purchases of land are certified by a notary.

44141.q: Does the duty to pay taxes violate the guarantee of ownership?
44141.e: The guarantee of ownership does not protect against taxes as long as they are based on a law and do not take away all of a person's wealth.
44141.m: Taxes do not violate the guarantee of ownership.

44142.q: Which code regulates ownership, possession and the land register in Switzerland?
44142.e: The Civil Code (ZGB) of 1907 contains property law with ownership, possession and the land register.

44143.q: Where is it recorded in Switzerland who owns a plot of land?
44143.e: The land register is a public register. It shows who owns a plot of land and which rights are attached to it.
44143.m: The land register shows who owns a plot of land.

44144.q: Who monitors prices in Switzerland in areas without effective competition?
44144.e: The Price Supervisor prevents unfair prices, for example for fees, electricity or medicines. He is informally called “Monsieur Prix”.
44144.m: The Price Supervisor protects against unfair prices.

44145.q: Who basically sets shop opening hours in Switzerland?
44145.e: Shop opening hours are regulated by the cantons. That is why they are not the same in all cantons.
44145.m: The cantons decide shop opening hours.

44146.q: Which right of the cantons restricts economic freedom when selling salt?
44146.e: The salt trade is a cantonal monopoly. The cantons have given this task to Schweizer Salinen AG.
44146.m: In Switzerland, salt is a monopoly of the cantons.

44147.q: What is an organisation called that stands up for the rights of employees?
44147.e: Employees may join together in trade unions. The Federal Constitution protects this with freedom of association.
44147.m: Trade unions stand up for employees.

44148.q: May a hairdresser with a qualification from Bern also work in Zurich?
a: Yes, the qualification is valid throughout Switzerland
No, only in the canton of Bern
Only with the Federal Council's permission
44148.e: The Internal Market Act makes sure that vocational qualifications are in principle valid throughout Switzerland.
44148.m: A Swiss vocational qualification is valid throughout Switzerland.

44152.q: Where do Swiss citizens in principle exercise their political rights?
44152.e: Article 39 paragraph 2 states that political rights are exercised at the place of residence. Anyone who moves then votes in their new municipality.
44152.m: You vote and elect where you live.

44153.q: What is the longest the cantons may make newcomers wait before they can vote on cantonal matters?
44153.e: According to Article 39 paragraph 4, cantons can set a waiting period of at most three months after a person settles there.
44153.m: The waiting period for voting after a move is at most three months.

44154.q: May Switzerland expel Swiss citizens from the country?
44154.e: Article 25 paragraph 1 states that Swiss citizens may not be expelled from Switzerland.
44154.m: Swiss citizens may not be expelled from Switzerland.

44155.q: According to the Civil Code, where is a person's place of residence?
a: Where they live intending to stay permanently
44155.e: Article 23 of the Civil Code defines the place of residence as the place where a person lives with the intention of staying permanently.
44155.m: Your place of residence is where you intend to live permanently.

44156.q: Between whom does the Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons apply?
44156.e: The Free Movement Agreement is part of the Bilateral Agreements I between Switzerland and the EU. It means that people from the EU and Switzerland can live and work in each other's territory.
44156.m: Free movement of persons applies between Switzerland and the EU.

44157.q: What is a person called who lives somewhere else during the week and returns home at the weekend?
44157.e: Weekly residents only register as weekly residents where they work or study. Their place of residence stays where they live at weekends.
44157.m: Weekly residents keep their place of residence where their family lives.

44158.q: Which obligation can restrict the freedom of residence of certain state employees?
44158.e: Municipalities or cantons can require certain employees to live near their workplace if there is a public interest, for example in the fire brigade.
44158.m: A residence requirement can restrict freedom of residence.

44159.q: Who does the freedom of residence in Article 24 of the Federal Constitution apply to?
44159.e: Article 24 is a citizen's right for Swiss nationals. For foreigners, laws and agreements such as free movement of persons apply.
44159.m: The constitution's freedom of residence applies to Swiss citizens.

44160.q: What did women's organisations submit a petition with about 250,000 signatures to the federal government for in 1929?
44160.e: In 1929 women's organisations handed the federal government a petition for women's right to vote. For a long time it had no effect, and the right to vote only came in 1971.
44160.m: As early as 1929 a large petition demanded women's right to vote.

44161.q: Is there a deadline within which signatures for a petition must be collected?
44161.e: There is no legal deadline for collecting signatures for petitions. For a popular initiative, on the other hand, the signatures must be gathered within 18 months.
44161.m: There is no deadline for collecting signatures for a petition.

44162.q: What is a person called who submits a petition?
44162.e: Anyone who submits a petition is called a petitioner.
44162.m: Anyone who submits a petition is a petitioner.

44163.q: Who first examines a petition to the Federal Assembly?
a: The President of the Confederation alone
44163.e: Petitions to parliament are assigned to a responsible committee. It can, for example, turn the petition into a parliamentary proposal.
44163.m: Petitions to parliament are first examined by a committee.

44164.q: In which part of the Federal Constitution is the right of petition?
a: In the chapter on fundamental rights
In the chapter on the army
44164.e: The right of petition is in the first chapter of the second title, among the fundamental rights (Articles 7 to 36).
44164.m: The right of petition is one of the fundamental rights.

44165.q: Who may sign a federal popular initiative, whereas a petition is open to everyone?
44165.e: Only people entitled to vote may sign a popular initiative. A petition, on the other hand, may be signed by anyone, including children.
44165.m: Only voters sign popular initiatives, but anyone can sign a petition.

44166.q: To which EU institution can EU citizens send petitions?
44166.e: Every EU citizen has the right to send a petition to the European Parliament. There a Committee on Petitions examines the submissions.
44166.m: In the EU, petitions are sent to the European Parliament.

44167.q: In what form do you submit a petition to an authority?
44167.e: A petition is a written submission to an authority. It can be submitted on paper or, today, often electronically too.
44167.m: You submit a petition in writing.

44168.q: Does an authority have to meet the demand of a petition?
a: No, it only has to take note of it
44168.e: A petition is not binding. The authority does have to take note of it, but it decides freely whether to do anything.
44168.m: A petition does not force the authority to act.

44169.q: Which feature characterises a presidential system of government?
a: Parliament cannot vote the government out for political reasons
The head of government is elected by parliament
The head of state is always a monarch
Government members must belong to parliament
44169.e: In a presidential system the executive and the legislature are independent of each other. The president has a fixed term and does not depend on the confidence of parliament.
44169.m: In a presidential system the government stays in office regardless of parliament's confidence.

44170.q: What can the US President NOT do towards Congress in the presidential system?
a: Dissolve Congress and call new elections
Nominate judges for the Supreme Court
Issue orders to the federal administration
44170.e: In the presidential system the President and Congress are elected for fixed terms. The President cannot dissolve Congress, just as Congress cannot remove him for political reasons.
44170.m: The US President has no right to dissolve Congress.

44171.q: Which offices does the President of the USA combine in one person?
a: Head of state and head of government
Head of government and speaker of parliament
Head of state and chief justice
Speaker of parliament and chief justice
44171.e: In the US presidential system there is no separate prime minister. The President represents the state and at the same time leads the government.
44171.m: The US President is head of state and head of government at once.

44172.q: Which chamber of the US Congress must approve the President's appointment of ministers and federal judges?
44172.e: The Constitution requires the “advice and consent” of the Senate for important appointments. This is how the legislature controls the President's choice of personnel.
44172.m: Important appointments by the US President need the Senate's approval.

44173.q: Which body formally elects the President of the USA?
44173.e: Citizens in the states vote for electors. These form the Electoral College, which formally elects the President.
44173.m: Formally, the Electoral College elects the President of the USA.

44174.q: With which instrument can the US President initially block a law passed by Congress?
44174.e: The President can refuse to sign a law. This right of veto is a key means of mutual control.
44174.m: With a veto the US President can hold up laws.

44175.q: What is it called in the USA when the President belongs to a different party from the majority in Congress?
44175.e: In a “divided government” the President has to work with an opposing majority. This is common in the presidential system because the President and Congress are elected separately.
44175.m: Divided government occurs when the President and Congress belong to different camps.

44176.q: What is the principle by which the branches of government limit and control each other in the presidential system?
44176.e: “Checks and balances” means that each branch has means to restrain the others, such as the veto, Senate approval or judicial review.
44176.m: Checks and balances ensure the branches control each other.

44177.q: In Britain, what is the team called with which the largest opposition party sets an opposite number against each minister?
44177.e: The opposition names a spokesperson for each ministry. This shadow cabinet is meant to show that it could govern itself at any time.
44177.m: With the shadow cabinet the opposition keeps a replacement government ready.

44178.q: What is Switzerland's system of government usually called in political science?
44178.e: The Federal Assembly elects the Federal Council but cannot remove it during its four-year term. The Federal Council is a collective body without a head of government, so it is called a directorial system.
44178.m: With the Federal Council, Switzerland has a directorial system.

44179.q: What can the British Prime Minister once again bring about since the Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022?
a: Early elections to the House of Commons
The abolition of the House of Lords
44179.e: The 2022 Act repealed the Fixed-term Parliaments Act 2011. Since then the monarch again dissolves Parliament at the Prime Minister's request, so the Prime Minister can largely decide the election date.
44179.m: The British Prime Minister can bring about early elections.

44180.q: Which body elects the German Federal President?
44180.e: The Federal Convention consists of all members of the Bundestag and an equal number of delegates from the states. It meets only to elect the head of state.
44180.m: The German Federal President is elected by the Federal Convention.

44181.q: Which term describes the close link between the government and the parliamentary majority in a parliamentary system?
44181.e: Government members are often also members of parliament, and the majority supports the government. Instead of strict separation, one therefore speaks of a fusion of powers.
44181.m: In a parliamentary system government and parliament are interlinked.

44182.q: In a parliamentary system, who mainly does the job of controlling the government in parliament?
44182.e: Because the parliamentary majority supports the government, critical scrutiny falls mainly to the opposition parties.
44182.m: In a parliamentary system it is mainly the opposition that controls the government.

44183.q: With which instrument can a head of government in a parliamentary system test whether they still have a majority?
44183.e: In a confidence vote the head of government themselves puts to the vote whether parliament trusts them. A vote of no confidence, by contrast, comes from parliament.
44183.m: With a confidence vote the government tests its majority.

44184.q: What characterises a semi-presidential system as in France?
a: A directly elected president and a government dependent on parliament
A king as head of state without power
A seven-member government without a president
A president who also heads parliament
44184.e: In semi-presidentialism a president elected by the people and a prime minister share power. The prime minister needs the confidence of parliament.
44184.m: In semi-presidentialism the president and prime minister share the executive.

44185.q: How long was the French President's term of office before the reform of 2000?
44185.e: From 1873 France had the “septennat”. Only a referendum in 2000 shortened the term, starting with the 2002 election.
44185.m: The French President used to serve for seven years.

44186.q: Which Nordic country clearly weakened the president's power with its 2000 constitution and has since been regarded as largely parliamentary?
44186.e: Finland long had a very strong, directly elected president. The 2000 constitution transferred many powers to the government and parliament.
44186.m: In 2000 Finland moved from semi-presidentialism to a parliamentary system.

44187.q: In which year was the President of France's Fifth Republic first elected directly by the people?
44187.e: A referendum in 1962 introduced direct election, and the first election under this procedure took place in 1965. Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte had already been directly elected as President of the Second Republic in 1848.
44187.m: In the Fifth Republic the President has been directly elected since 1965.

44188.q: What is the name of the French President's official residence in Paris?
44188.e: The President resides in the Élysée Palace. The Hôtel Matignon is the seat of the Prime Minister, and the National Assembly meets in the Palais Bourbon.
44188.m: The French President works in the Élysée Palace.

44189.q: What is the maximum number of rounds in the French presidential election?
44189.e: If nobody wins an absolute majority in the first round, the two leading candidates face each other in a run-off two weeks later.
44189.m: The French President is elected in no more than two rounds.

44190.q: Which chamber of the French parliament can bring down the government with a motion of censure?
44190.e: Only the directly elected National Assembly can force the government to resign with a “motion de censure”. The Senate does not have this right.
44190.m: In France only the National Assembly can bring down the government.

44191.q: Which European country besides France is often classified as semi-presidential?
44191.e: In Portugal the president is directly elected and has his own powers, while the government depends on parliament.
44191.m: Portugal is also regarded as a semi-presidential system.

44192.q: What is meant by cohabitation in France?
a: The president and prime minister come from opposing political camps
Two parties govern together in a coalition
The president and parliament are elected on the same day
44192.e: If the parliamentary majority leans differently from the president, he must appoint a prime minister from that camp. Both then have to work together.
44192.m: In cohabitation a president and a prime minister from different camps govern.

44193.q: Who was Prime Minister during the first cohabitation from 1986 to 1988?
44193.e: After the centre-right won the election in 1986, the Socialist President François Mitterrand appointed the Gaullist Jacques Chirac as Prime Minister.
44193.m: Jacques Chirac led the first cohabitation as Prime Minister.

44194.q: Who was Prime Minister during the second cohabitation from 1993 to 1995?
44194.e: After the right's clear election victory in 1993, the Gaullist Édouard Balladur became Prime Minister under a Socialist president.
44194.m: Édouard Balladur shaped the second cohabitation.

44195.q: Who was Prime Minister during the cohabitation from 1997 to 2002?
44195.e: After the early election of 1997 the left won, and the Socialist Lionel Jospin governed for five years alongside a centre-right president.
44195.m: Lionel Jospin was Prime Minister in the longest cohabitation.

44196.q: How many times was there a cohabitation in the Fifth Republic up to 2025?
44196.e: There were cohabitations from 1986 to 1988, 1993 to 1995 and 1997 to 2002. After that there were none up to 2025.
44196.m: France experienced three cohabitations up to 2025.

44197.q: Which reform made cohabitation in France much less likely from 2002?
a: Shortening the President's term to five years
44197.e: With the “quinquennat”, the presidential term and the parliamentary term are the same length, and the parliamentary election follows shortly after the presidential one. Voters therefore usually give the new president a majority.
44197.m: Since the quinquennat, cohabitations have been rare in France.

44198.q: Which policy areas are traditionally regarded in France as the President's “domaine réservé”?
44198.e: The President is commander-in-chief of the armed forces and represents France internationally. He largely keeps these areas even when parliament has an opposing majority.
44198.m: Foreign and defence policy remain the President's business in France.

44199.q: Who mainly decides France's domestic policy during a cohabitation?
a: The Prime Minister with his parliamentary majority
44199.e: Under Article 20 of the constitution the government determines the policy of the nation. With an opposing majority, the President therefore loses influence over most domestic issues.
44199.m: In cohabitation the Prime Minister steers domestic policy.

44200.q: What majority does the Bundestag need to elect a new chancellor through a constructive vote of no confidence?
44200.e: What is needed is a majority of the statutory members, the so-called chancellor majority. Abstentions and absent members therefore count like no votes.
44200.m: A constructive vote of no confidence needs the chancellor majority.

44201.q: What must the Bundestag do at the same time in a constructive vote of no confidence?
a: Vote out each cabinet member individually
44201.e: Under Article 67 of the Basic Law the Bundestag can only express no confidence in the chancellor by electing a successor. That way there is no gap in government.
44201.m: Anyone who wants to topple the chancellor must elect a new one straight away.

44202.q: How many times up to 2025 did the Bundestag vote on a constructive vote of no confidence?
44202.e: Votes were held in 1972 and 1982. Only the second attempt succeeded and led to a change of chancellor.
44202.m: Up to 2025 the Bundestag held two votes on a constructive vote of no confidence.

44203.q: Which German chancellor only narrowly survived a constructive vote of no confidence in 1972?
44203.e: The challenger Rainer Barzel (CDU) missed the required majority by two votes. Later one member of parliament admitted to having received money for abstaining.
44203.m: Willy Brandt narrowly survived a vote of no confidence in 1972.

44204.q: Which historical experience led to the constructive vote of no confidence being included in the Basic Law?
a: The unstable governments of the Weimar Republic
The founding of the German Empire
44204.e: In the Weimar Republic opposing parties could join forces to topple governments without forming an alternative themselves. This was not to happen again.
44204.m: The constructive vote of no confidence grew out of the Weimar experience.

44205.q: Why does the Basic Law require a waiting period between the motion and the vote in a vote of no confidence?
a: So that members have time to think
So that the people can vote first
So that the Bundesrat can agree
So that new members can be elected
44205.e: Article 67 of the Basic Law requires 48 hours between the motion and the vote. This is meant to prevent rash decisions.
44205.m: There are 48 hours between the motion and the vote of no confidence.

44206.q: In which country was the head of government replaced through a constructive vote of no confidence in 2018?
44206.e: In June 2018 the Spanish parliament replaced Mariano Rajoy with Pedro Sánchez. The Spanish constitution also has the constructive form of the “moción de censura”.
44206.m: Spain also has the constructive vote of no confidence.

44207.q: What is the form of no-confidence vote called in which a government can be toppled without electing a successor?
44207.e: In a destructive, or simple, vote of no confidence a majority against the government is enough. Whether a new majority then forms remains open.
44207.m: A destructive vote of no confidence topples a government without a successor.

44208.q: Who wins a constituency under first-past-the-post (relative majority) voting?
a: Whoever gets over 50 per cent of the votes
Whoever gets the most second votes
44208.e: With a relative majority it is enough to be ahead of everyone else. An absolute majority is not needed.
44208.m: With relative majority voting, whoever has the most votes wins.

44209.q: Where does the English expression “first past the post” come from?
44209.e: As in a horse race, the winner is whoever reaches the finishing post first. The gap to the others does not matter.
44209.m: First past the post compares the election to a horse race.

44210.q: In which year did British voters reject switching from “first past the post” to the “alternative vote” in a referendum?
44210.e: In the referendum of May 2011 about two thirds voted against the alternative vote. So first past the post remained in place for the House of Commons.
44210.m: In 2011 Britain kept first past the post by referendum.

44211.q: How many seats are usually awarded per constituency under “first past the post”?
a: As many as there are parties standing
44211.e: The system uses single-member constituencies: each constituency sends exactly one person to parliament.
44211.m: First past the post awards one seat per constituency.

44212.q: In a constituency, A gets 40 per cent, B 35 per cent and C 25 per cent. What percentage of voters did not vote for the winner?
44212.e: A wins with 40 per cent. Against A voted 35 + 25 = 60 per cent, which is a majority.
44212.m: With relative majority voting, a minority of the votes can be enough to win.

44213.q: With roughly what percentage of the vote did the Labour Party win almost two thirds of the seats in the House of Commons in 2024?
44213.e: In 2024 Labour received about 33.7 per cent of the vote but 411 of 650 seats. This shows how disproportional the system is.
44213.m: Majority voting can turn a third of the votes into a large majority of seats.

44214.q: How does absolute majority voting differ from relative majority voting?
a: If no one gets over 50 per cent, another round follows
Several seats are awarded per constituency
Seats are distributed by party lists
44214.e: With absolute majority voting, for example for the French National Assembly, you need more than half the votes in the first round. Otherwise there is a second round.
44214.m: Absolute majority voting requires over half the votes or another round.

44215.q: What are votes called that go to losing candidates in majority voting and win no seat?
44215.e: All votes for losers in a constituency have no effect on the distribution of seats. They are called wasted votes.
44215.m: In majority voting, votes for constituency losers are wasted.

44216.q: By which method is the National Council elected in cantons with only one seat, such as Uri or Glarus?
a: Absolute majority voting with a run-off
44216.e: If only one seat is to be filled, the Federal Act on Political Rights says whoever gets the most votes is elected. Proportional representation is not possible with one seat.
44216.m: In cantons with one National Council seat, relative majority voting applies.

44217.q: What do voters use their first vote for in the German Bundestag election?
44217.e: With the first vote a person is elected in the constituency. This element makes the proportional system “personalised”.
44217.m: The first vote goes to a person in the constituency.

44218.q: What is the Sainte-Laguë method used for in the German Bundestag election?
a: For distributing seats among the parties
44218.e: Since the 2009 election, seats have been distributed among the parties using the Sainte-Laguë method. Before that, the Hare-Niemeyer method was used.
44218.m: The Bundestag distributes its seats using the Sainte-Laguë method.

a: Constituency seats beyond the number a party is due by its second votes
Seats for parties below the threshold
Seats that become free after resignations
44219.e: If a party in a state won more constituencies than it was due seats by its second votes, overhang seats used to arise. This made the Bundestag bigger.
44219.m: Overhang seats arise from too many constituency seats.

44220.q: What was the purpose of balancing seats in German Bundestag electoral law from 2013 to 2023?
a: They restored proportionality after overhang seats
They gave small parties a seat
They gave every state the same number of seats
44220.e: If a party received overhang seats, the others got extra seats. That way the overall result matched the second votes again, but the Bundestag grew considerably.
44220.m: Balancing seats evened out distortions caused by overhang seats.

44221.q: What was the main aim of the German electoral reform of 2023?
a: To lower the voting age to 14
44221.e: Because of overhang and balancing seats, the Bundestag had grown to 736 members. The reform limits it to 630 seats.
44221.m: The 2023 reform was meant to make the Bundestag smaller.

44222.q: Since the 2023 electoral reform, what applies to constituency winners in the Bundestag election?
a: They only get the seat if it is covered by their party's second-vote result
They always get an extra seat
They must win over 50 per cent of the first votes
They are confirmed by the Bundesrat
44222.e: Under the principle of second-vote coverage, a party gets at most as many seats as it is due by its second votes. Constituency winners with the weakest results can miss out.
44222.m: Since 2023, constituency seats must be covered by second votes.

44223.q: How many people are elected with the first vote in a German Bundestag constituency?
a: As many as there are parties standing
44223.e: Germany is divided into 299 constituencies. In each one exactly one person is elected with the first vote.
44223.m: With the first vote, one person is elected per constituency.

44224.q: What is it called when someone gives their first and second votes to different parties?
44224.e: In vote splitting, someone might vote for a big party's constituency candidate and give their second vote to a possible coalition partner.
44224.m: Anyone who splits their first and second votes is vote splitting.

44225.q: Which country introduced an electoral system modelled on Germany's personalised proportional representation in 1996?
44225.e: After a referendum, New Zealand voted for the first time in 1996 under the “mixed member proportional” system with an electorate vote and a party vote.
44225.m: In 1996 New Zealand adopted the German model of proportional representation.

44226.q: What is the main purpose of an electoral threshold in proportional elections?
a: To give special support to small parties
To reduce the number of constituencies
44226.e: Parties below a minimum share get no seats. This is meant to make stable majorities and effective governments easier to form.
44226.m: A threshold is meant to prevent a splintered parliament.

44227.q: Why was there no electoral threshold in Germany for the 2024 European election?
a: The Federal Constitutional Court had declared the three per cent threshold unconstitutional in 2014
The EU bans thresholds in principle
The Bundestag had abolished the European election
European elections use relative majority voting
44227.e: Karlsruhe found the equal opportunities of parties violated, because the European Parliament does not have to support a government. That is why even very small parties get in from Germany.
44227.m: In the 2024 European election there was no threshold in Germany.

44228.q: Under the basic mandate clause, how many constituency seats does a party need to enter the Bundestag despite getting less than 5 per cent (as of 2025)?
44228.e: If a party wins at least three constituencies, it is counted according to its share of second votes. In 2024 the Federal Constitutional Court let this clause remain in force until new rules are made.
44228.m: With three constituency seats a party overcomes the threshold.

44229.q: Which party is exempt from the five per cent threshold in the Bundestag election as a party of a national minority?
44229.e: The SSW represents the Danish minority and the Frisians in Schleswig-Holstein. Parties of national minorities are exempt from the threshold.
44229.m: As a minority party, the SSW is exempt from the threshold.

44230.q: How high is the threshold in the German Bundestag election?
44230.e: Parties with less than 5 per cent of the second votes generally get no seats. Exceptions apply, for example, to parties of national minorities.
44230.m: The Bundestag has a five per cent threshold.

44231.q: How high was Turkey's electoral threshold until 2022, considered one of the highest in Europe?
44231.e: Turkey's ten per cent threshold applied for decades. In 2022 it was lowered to 7 per cent.
44231.m: Turkey long had a ten per cent threshold.

44232.q: Why can there be a high hurdle in National Council elections in small cantons even though there is no legal threshold?
a: Because only a few seats are distributed there
Because small parties are not allowed to stand
Because the Federal Council sets a minimum size
44232.e: Each canton is its own constituency. With few seats, a list needs a high share of the vote to win a seat; this is called a natural or effective threshold.
44232.m: Few seats per canton create an effective threshold.

44233.q: Which party only very narrowly missed the threshold in the 2025 Bundestag election, with just under 5 per cent?
44233.e: The BSW got 4.981 per cent of the second votes, only about 0.02 percentage points too few. It therefore did not enter the Bundestag.
44233.m: In 2025 the BSW missed the Bundestag by a hair's breadth.

44234.q: Parties below the threshold together receive 15 per cent of the votes. What share of seats does a party with 42.5 per cent get if the seats are shared proportionally among the rest?
44234.e: Only the 85 per cent of valid votes for parties above the threshold count. 42.5 : 85 = 0.5, so 50 per cent of the seats.
44234.m: Thresholds increase the share of seats of the successful parties.

44235.q: According to Duverger's law, which party system does relative majority voting in single-member constituencies favour?
44235.e: If only the person with the most votes wins in each constituency, small parties hardly stand a chance. Voters and parties therefore concentrate on two big camps.
44235.m: According to Duverger, relative majority voting favours two big parties.

44236.q: What effect did Duverger attribute to two-round majority voting, as used in France?
a: It favours several parties that form alliances before the run-off
It inevitably leads to a one-party system
It works exactly like relative majority voting
It prevents any kind of party alliance
44236.e: Duverger suspected that run-off systems allow many parties that join together in blocs before the second round. This is also called Duverger's hypothesis.
44236.m: According to Duverger, majority voting with a run-off favours party alliances.

44237.q: What effect did Duverger attribute to proportional representation?
a: It leads to a one-party system
It automatically creates two big parties
44237.e: Because smaller parties also win seats under proportional representation, it is worth their while to stand. Several relevant parties emerge.
44237.m: According to Duverger, proportional representation encourages many parties.

44238.q: What does the “mechanical effect” describe in Duverger's theory?
a: Third parties receive far fewer seats than votes when seats are allocated
Voters switch their vote for tactical reasons
44238.e: Smaller parties hardly win any constituencies despite many votes, because they rarely come first. So the electoral system itself puts them at a disadvantage.
44238.m: The mechanical effect directly disadvantages third parties when seats are allocated.

44239.q: What does the “psychological effect” describe in Duverger's theory?
a: Voters vote for candidates with a real chance so as not to waste their vote
Candidates are elected for their personality
Polls decide the outcome of the election
44239.e: Many voters know that small parties hardly ever win. They therefore vote strategically for the “lesser evil” among the favourites.
44239.m: The psychological effect leads to tactical voting.

44240.q: Why are there more than two parties in Canada's parliament despite relative majority voting?
a: Regionally concentrated parties can win many constituencies
Canada uses a five per cent threshold
Seats are distributed by second votes
44240.e: Parties such as the Bloc Québécois are strong in one region and win constituencies there. Duverger's law applies mainly at constituency level, not necessarily nationwide.

44241.q: Which country is often cited as an example of Duverger's law at work, because two parties have dominated there for a long time?
44241.e: In the USA the Democrats and Republicans have dominated for more than 150 years. Third parties hardly win any seats in Congress in majority elections.
44241.m: The USA shows the two-party system described by Duverger particularly clearly.

44242.q: In which work did Duverger describe the link between electoral system and party system in 1951?
44242.e: In “Les partis politiques” (1951) Duverger set out his theses on the effects of electoral systems. The other works are by Rousseau, Montesquieu and Tocqueville.
44242.m: Duverger's main work is called “Les partis politiques”.

a: Deliberately drawing constituency boundaries to favour one party
44243.e: By cleverly drawing boundaries, a party can win more constituencies with the same number of votes. The practice is best known from the USA.

a: Gerald Ford, President of the USA
44244.e: In 1812 Governor Elbridge Gerry signed a law with a strangely shaped constituency that favoured his party.
44244.m: Elbridge Gerry gave gerrymandering its name.

44245.q: Where does the second part of the word gerrymandering come from?
a: From the salamander, which a constituency resembled
From the mandarin, a Chinese official
From the name of a newspaper publisher
44245.e: In 1812 a newspaper compared the winding constituency to a salamander. Gerry and salamander became “gerrymander”.
44245.m: The word gerrymandering combines a name with the salamander.

44246.q: What is the technique called in which the opponent's supporters are spread over many constituencies so that they win nowhere?
44246.e: In cracking, the opposing electorate is split up. In every constituency it remains a minority.

44247.q: What is the technique called in which the opponent's supporters are concentrated in a few constituencies?
44247.e: In packing, the opponent wins a few constituencies by a huge margin. Its surplus votes are then missing in the other constituencies.
44247.m: Packing bundles the opponent's voters into a few constituencies.

44248.q: 50 voters are divided into 5 constituencies of 10 people each; 30 vote for party A, 20 for party B. With clever boundaries, what is the most constituencies B can win?
44248.e: To win, B needs at least 6 out of 10 votes. 3 × 6 = 18 is possible, but 4 × 6 = 24 is more than B's 20 votes.
44248.m: With clever boundaries a minority can win most of the constituencies.

44249.q: How often are the districts of the US House of Representatives usually redrawn?
a: Every 4 years with the presidential election
Only when the constitution is amended
44249.e: After each census the seats are distributed among the states and the districts are redrawn. This process is called redistricting.
44249.m: US districts are redrawn after every census.

44250.q: What measure do some US states such as California use against gerrymandering?
a: An independent commission draws the district boundaries
The districts are drawn by lot every year
There is only one district per state
44250.e: In California a citizens' commission sets the boundaries, not the legislature. This is meant to reduce the influence of the parties.
44250.m: Independent commissions are meant to prevent gerrymandering.

44251.q: What did the US Supreme Court decide in 2019 in the case “Rucho v. Common Cause”?
a: Federal courts cannot review partisan gerrymandering
Gerrymandering is banned in all states
Congress must draw the districts itself
44251.e: The court declared partisan gerrymandering a political question. Federal courts were not responsible for it, but the states and Congress were.
44251.m: Since 2019 US federal courts no longer review partisan gerrymandering.

44252.q: What is a coalition called that includes more parties than would be needed for a majority?
44252.e: An oversized coalition (“surplus majority”) contains at least one partner without which it would still have a majority. It can make sense, for example, for constitutional changes or broad support.
44252.m: An oversized coalition has more partners than necessary.

44253.q: In Germany, what is the body called in which the leaders of the governing parties settle disputes outside the cabinet?
44253.e: The coalition committee brings together party leaders, parliamentary group leaders and leading government members. It is not provided for in the Basic Law, but it is politically very influential.
44253.m: Disputes in German coalitions are often settled in the coalition committee.

44254.q: What is a coalition called that would lose its majority as soon as any one partner left?
44254.e: The theory of the “minimal winning coalition” goes back to William Riker. It has no unnecessary partners, because that way power is shared among fewer parties.
44254.m: A minimal winning coalition has no unnecessary partner.

44255.q: According to coalition research, which parties are most likely to join together to form a government?
a: Parties from the far left and far right
44255.e: Robert Axelrod spoke of a connected coalition: partners that sit next to each other on the left-right scale find a common policy more easily.
44255.m: A connected coalition is made up of politically neighbouring parties.

44256.q: Under which German chancellor did a three-party coalition collapse in November 2024?
44256.e: The coalition collapsed after Finance Minister Christian Lindner (FDP) was dismissed. An early Bundestag election followed in February 2025.
44256.m: Olaf Scholz's coalition collapsed in November 2024.

44257.q: Which parties form the Austrian federal government that was sworn in in March 2025?
44257.e: After the 2024 National Council election, talks between the FPÖ and ÖVP failed. Under Chancellor Christian Stocker, three parties are governing together for the first time since 1947.
44257.m: Since March 2025 Austria has been governed by the ÖVP, SPÖ and NEOS.

44258.q: A parliament has 100 seats: A 45, B 30, C 15, D 10. Which two-party coalition has the narrowest absolute majority?
44258.e: At least 51 seats are needed. A and D have 55, A and C 60, A and B 75; B and C reach only 45.
44258.m: For a majority a coalition needs more than half the seats.

44259.q: Which country needed about 541 days after the 2010 parliamentary election to form a new government?
44259.e: The conflict between Flemish and French-speaking parties made forming a coalition difficult. Only at the end of 2011 did the Di Rupo government take office.
44259.m: Belgium is known for very long government formations.

44260.q: Which party made a support agreement in 2022 with Justin Trudeau's Liberal minority government in Canada?
44260.e: The “Supply and Confidence Agreement” of March 2022 secured the government's votes on the budget and in confidence votes. The NDP ended it in September 2024.
44260.m: In Canada the NDP supported the Trudeau minority government from 2022.

44261.q: What is it called when a party supports a minority government without being part of it?
44261.e: A tolerating party provides no ministers but, for example, votes with the government on the budget or refrains from a vote of no confidence.
44261.m: In toleration a party supports the government from outside.

44262.q: How does a minority government without fixed support find majorities in parliament?
a: With changing majorities case by case
Through emergency decrees of the head of state
By excluding the opposition from votes
44262.e: For each project the government looks for suitable partners. That requires compromise but often makes governing uncertain.
44262.m: Minority governments often work with changing majorities.

44263.q: In which country have minority governments been especially common for decades?
44263.e: In Denmark most governments since the Second World War have had no majority of their own in the Folketing. They work with fixed agreements and changing majorities.
44263.m: Denmark is a country of minority governments.

44264.q: Which party supports the Swedish minority government under Ulf Kristersson (since 2022) in the Tidö Agreement without providing ministers?
44264.e: In 2022 the government of Moderates, Christian Democrats and Liberals made an agreement with the Sweden Democrats at Tidö Castle. They support the government in the Riksdag.
44264.m: In Sweden the Sweden Democrats support the government from outside.

44265.q: Which German state has been governed by a CDU and SPD minority government since December 2024?
44265.e: After the 2024 state election, Michael Kretschmer formed a government of CDU and SPD, which has 51 of 120 seats.
44265.m: Saxony has had a minority government since 2024.

44266.q: A minority government has 85 of 200 seats. With everyone present, how many more votes does it need at least for an absolute majority?
44266.e: A majority of 200 seats is 101 votes. 101 minus 85 = 16 extra votes.
44266.m: A minority government needs other parties' votes for every vote.

44267.q: Which party supported Theresa May's British minority government in 2017 with an agreement on confidence and the budget?
44267.e: After losing their majority in 2017, the Conservatives made a “confidence and supply” agreement with Northern Ireland's DUP and its ten MPs.
44267.m: From 2017 Theresa May governed with the support of the DUP.

44268.q: What is the title of the person who leads the US House of Representatives?
44268.e: The Speaker is elected by the members and leads the chamber. In the presidential line of succession the Speaker comes second, after the Vice President.
