44503.m: Separation of powers and fundamental rights belong to every true constitution.

44504.q: In which city was the European Convention on Human Rights signed in 1950?
44504.e: The member states of the Council of Europe signed the Convention in Rome on 4 November 1950.
44504.m: The ECHR was signed in Rome in 1950.

44505.q: Which international organisation is behind the European Convention on Human Rights?
44505.e: The ECHR is a treaty of the Council of Europe, which was founded in 1949. It must be distinguished from the European Union.
44505.m: The ECHR belongs to the Council of Europe, not the EU.

44506.q: Which fundamental right does Article 3 of the ECHR protect without any exception?
44506.e: Article 3 forbids torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. The ban is absolute, even in war or a state of emergency.
44506.m: The ECHR's ban on torture has no exceptions.

44507.q: What condition must an individual usually meet before they can bring a complaint in Strasbourg?
a: Use up all domestic legal remedies
The consent of their own government
44507.e: The Court only examines a case if it has first gone through all national courts. In Switzerland that is usually the Federal Supreme Court.
44507.m: Before going to Strasbourg you must go through the courts in your own country.

44508.q: Which right does the ECHR guarantee with, among other things, the presumption of innocence and an independent court?
a: The right to a fair trial
44508.e: Art. 6 ECHR ensures an independent court, a public hearing within a reasonable time and the presumption of innocence.
44508.m: The ECHR guarantees a fair trial.

44509.q: Which Swiss association won a climate case before the European Court of Human Rights in 2024?
44509.e: In April 2024 the Court found that Switzerland had violated Art. 8 ECHR through insufficient climate protection.
44509.m: With the KlimaSeniorinnen ruling, the Court found a breach of the ECHR because of insufficient climate protection for the first time.

44510.q: What does Protocol No. 13 to the ECHR, which Switzerland has also ratified, forbid?
a: The death penalty in all circumstances
The death penalty only in peacetime
44510.e: Protocol No. 6 at first banned the death penalty only in peacetime. Protocol No. 13 bans it without exception, so in war too.
44510.m: Protocol No. 13 bans the death penalty without exception.

44511.q: Where are the fundamental rights found in the Swiss Federal Constitution?
a: Near the beginning, after the general provisions
Right at the end in the transitional provisions
Nowhere, only in the Civil Code
44511.e: After the general provisions, Title 2 contains the list of fundamental rights (Art. 7 to 36). It begins with human dignity.
44511.m: The fundamental rights are near the front of the Federal Constitution.

44512.q: With which fundamental right does the list of fundamental rights in the Federal Constitution begin, in Art. 7?
44512.e: Art. 7 of the Federal Constitution reads: “Human dignity must be respected and protected.” It is the basis of all other fundamental rights.
44512.m: Human dignity is at the start of the list of fundamental rights.

44513.q: What does Art. 10 para. 1 of the Federal Constitution expressly forbid?
44513.e: Art. 10 of the Federal Constitution protects the right to life. Paragraph 1 states that the death penalty is prohibited.
44513.m: The Federal Constitution forbids the death penalty.

44514.q: Which fundamental right protects the use of your own mother tongue?
44514.e: Freedom of language (Art. 18 of the Federal Constitution) protects the use of your own language, especially your mother tongue, in private life.
44514.m: Everyone in Switzerland may use their own language.

44515.q: Which social right does Art. 19 of the Federal Constitution guarantee?
44515.e: The cantons must offer all children adequate basic education free of charge.
44515.m: Under the constitution, basic education in Switzerland is free.

44516.q: Which fundamental right in the Federal Constitution is reserved for Swiss citizens only?
44516.e: Art. 24 of the Federal Constitution allows Swiss nationals to settle anywhere in the country and to leave the country. For others, laws and agreements apply.
44516.m: Freedom of residence is a civil right of Swiss citizens.

44517.q: What does Art. 35 of the Federal Constitution require of everyone who carries out state tasks?
a: They are bound by fundamental rights
44517.e: Art. 35 of the Federal Constitution requires that fundamental rights be upheld throughout the legal system. Anyone who carries out state tasks must respect them and help put them into practice.
44517.m: Anyone who carries out state tasks must respect fundamental rights.

44518.q: Why can the Federal Supreme Court not strike down a federal act even if it violates fundamental rights?
a: Federal acts are binding under Art. 190 of the Federal Constitution
Federal acts only apply for a limited time
The Federal Supreme Court is only responsible for criminal law
Federal acts are subject to the UN
44518.e: Art. 190 of the Federal Constitution obliges the courts to apply federal acts. Switzerland therefore has no constitutional review of federal acts.
44518.m: Courts must apply federal acts, even if they are problematic.

44519.q: Which fundamental right does Art. 17 of the Federal Constitution protect, banning censorship?
44519.e: Art. 17 of the Federal Constitution guarantees the freedom of the press, radio and television, bans censorship and protects editorial secrecy.
44519.m: Media freedom protects the press, radio and television from censorship.

44520.q: Under Art. 36 of the Federal Constitution, what legal basis is enough for a minor restriction of a fundamental right?
44520.e: Minor restrictions may be based on a law in the material sense, which includes an ordinance of the government. Only serious restrictions need an act passed by parliament.
44520.m: An ordinance is enough for minor restrictions of fundamental rights.

44521.q: Under Art. 36 of the Federal Constitution, what basis does a serious restriction of a fundamental right need?
a: A law in the formal sense
44521.e: Serious restrictions must be laid down in the act itself, which was passed by parliament and is subject to referendum.
44521.m: The more serious a restriction of fundamental rights, the more clearly a law must regulate it.

44522.q: In which case does Art. 36 of the Federal Constitution allow a restriction of fundamental rights without a legal basis?
a: In case of serious, immediate danger that cannot be averted otherwise
With a majority in the municipal council
44522.e: This exception is called the general police clause. It only applies to real emergencies that lawmakers could not foresee.
44522.m: Only in real emergencies may the state restrict fundamental rights without a law.

44523.q: Which court in Switzerland decides as the highest authority whether cantonal authorities have violated a fundamental right?
a: The High Court of the Canton of Bern
44523.e: The Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne is the highest court in Switzerland. Anyone who feels their fundamental rights have been violated can take the case all the way there.
44523.m: The Federal Supreme Court has the final say on violations of fundamental rights.

44524.q: Besides the public interest, what is an allowed reason for restricting a fundamental right?
a: Protecting the fundamental rights of others
44524.e: The fundamental rights of different people can clash, for example freedom of expression and protection of personality. Then one may be restricted in favour of the other.
44524.m: Fundamental rights can be restricted to protect the rights of others.

44525.q: What does Art. 36 para. 4 of the Federal Constitution lay down to protect fundamental rights?
a: The essence of fundamental rights is inviolable.
Fundamental rights apply only to Swiss citizens.
Emergency law may cancel all fundamental rights.
Fundamental rights bind only the cantons.
44525.e: Even if the other conditions of Art. 36 are met, a restriction may never touch the essence of a fundamental right. This innermost core is beyond any weighing up.
44525.m: The state may never violate the essence of a fundamental right.

44526.q: What does a court examine under the heading “public interest” when a fundamental right is restricted?
a: Whether the restriction serves a legitimate aim of the community
Whether the majority likes the restriction
Whether the restriction brings in money
44526.e: Allowed aims include, for example, public safety, health, environmental protection or peace and order. Purely financial interests are usually not enough.
44526.m: Restricting a fundamental right needs a legitimate aim in the interest of the community.

44527.q: Which restriction of fundamental rights during the Covid-19 pandemic was based, among other things, on the Epidemics Act?
a: Abolition of the right to vote
44527.e: The Confederation and the cantons restricted freedom of assembly and economic freedom, based on the Epidemics Act and emergency ordinances.
44527.m: Even in the pandemic, restrictions of fundamental rights needed a legal basis.

44528.q: Which three parts does the principle of proportionality include?
44528.e: A measure must be able to achieve its aim, be the mildest effective means and stand in reasonable relation to the restriction.
44528.m: A measure is only proportionate if it is suitable, necessary and reasonable.

44529.q: Where in Switzerland is it laid down that all state action must be proportionate?
44529.e: Art. 5 para. 2 of the Federal Constitution requires state action to be in the public interest and proportionate.
44529.m: All state action must be proportionate.

44530.q: What does the necessity test examine?
a: Whether there is no milder, equally effective means
Whether the measure has been used before
44530.e: If there is a means that achieves the aim just as well with less interference, the stricter measure is not necessary.
44530.m: The state must choose the mildest effective means.

44531.q: Which saying describes a breach of the principle of proportionality?
a: To use a sledgehammer to crack a nut
To set the fox to guard the henhouse
To buy a pig in a poke
To not see the wood for the trees
44531.e: The saying describes a means that is far too strong for the aim being pursued.
44531.m: Too strong a means for a small problem is disproportionate.

44532.q: Because of a single noise complaint, a municipality bans all concerts for a year. Which part of the test is most clearly violated?
44532.e: The ban would prevent noise, but milder means such as time limits or volume restrictions would be enough.
44532.m: If milder conditions are enough, a total ban is not necessary.

44533.q: What is the test called that checks whether the restriction and the benefit are in reasonable proportion?
44533.e: This part is also called reasonableness. It weighs the public interest against the interests of the person affected.
44533.m: With reasonableness, public and private interests are weighed against each other.

44534.q: Under the suitability test, when is a measure disproportionate?
a: When it cannot achieve the aim at all
When it is put into practice too slowly
When it affects only a few people
44534.e: A measure that is unfit to achieve the intended aim may not be ordered.
44534.m: An unfit measure is never proportionate.

44535.q: Which fundamental right of the Federal Constitution does the prohibition of discrimination belong to?
44535.e: Art. 8 of the Federal Constitution deals with equality before the law. Paragraph 2 lists characteristics such as origin, sex, age, language or religion on which no one may be discriminated against.
44535.m: The prohibition of discrimination is part of the article on equality before the law.

44536.q: What does Art. 8 para. 3 of the Federal Constitution guarantee about the pay of women and men?
a: Equal pay for work of equal value
44536.e: Art. 8 para. 3 of the Federal Constitution requires equality in law and in fact. Women and men are entitled to equal pay for work of equal value.
44536.m: For work of equal value, women and men are entitled to the same pay.

44537.q: What is meant by indirect discrimination?
a: A neutral rule particularly disadvantages one group
44537.e: A rule is worded neutrally but affects a protected group much more negatively, for example worse treatment of part-time work that disadvantages women.
44537.m: Even seemingly neutral rules can discriminate.

44538.q: What does the anti-racism criminal provision in Switzerland make punishable?
a: Public incitement on grounds of race, ethnicity or religion
44538.e: Art. 261bis of the Criminal Code was approved by the people in 1994 and came into force in 1995. Public incitement or degradation is punishable, while factual criticism remains allowed.
44538.m: Racist incitement is a criminal offence in Switzerland.

44539.q: Which characteristic was added to the anti-racism criminal provision after the referendum of February 2020?
44539.e: Voters approved the extension with just over 63 per cent. Since then incitement on grounds of sexual orientation has also been punishable.
44539.m: Since 2020 criminal law also protects against incitement on grounds of sexual orientation.

44540.q: Which UN convention did Switzerland join in 1994, creating the anti-racism criminal provision for it?
a: Convention on the Rights of the Child
Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities
44540.e: The 1965 UN Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination requires racist incitement to be made a criminal offence. Switzerland therefore changed its Criminal Code.
44540.m: The anti-racism criminal provision goes back to a UN convention.

44541.q: What is special about the prohibition of discrimination in the ECHR?
a: It applies only together with another Convention right
44541.e: Art. 14 ECHR forbids discrimination only in the enjoyment of the rights the Convention guarantees. A general ban on discrimination only comes with Protocol No. 12, which Switzerland has not ratified.
44541.m: The ECHR's ban on discrimination applies to the Convention rights.

44542.q: When did the Federal Act on Gender Equality come into force?
44542.e: The Gender Equality Act came into force on 1 July 1996. It puts equality into concrete terms, above all in working life.
44542.m: The Gender Equality Act has applied since 1996.

44543.q: Which area of life does the Gender Equality Act mainly concern?
44543.e: It bans discrimination in hiring, pay, further training, promotion and dismissal.
44543.m: The Gender Equality Act gives protection mainly at work.

44544.q: What easing of the burden of proof does the Gender Equality Act provide for pay discrimination?
a: Discrimination only has to be shown to be likely
The employer never has to prove anything
44544.e: If the person affected shows that discrimination is likely, the employer must prove that there is none.
44544.m: In pay discrimination it is enough to show that the suspicion is credible.

44545.q: Since 2020, from how many employees must employers carry out an equal pay analysis?
44545.e: Since the revision of 1 July 2020, employers with at least 100 employees must analyse their pay and have it checked independently.
44545.m: Larger employers must regularly check for equal pay.

44546.q: Which behaviour at work is expressly regarded as discrimination under the Gender Equality Act?
44546.e: Art. 4 of the Gender Equality Act counts sexual harassment as discrimination. Employers must take steps to prevent it.
44546.m: Sexual harassment at work is a form of discrimination.

44547.q: Which federal office works to put equality between women and men into practice?
44547.e: The office, known by its German abbreviation EBG, provides information, supports projects and offers tools such as the pay analysis tool Logib.
44547.m: The EBG is the Confederation's specialist office for gender equality.

44548.q: Under the Gender Equality Act, what protection applies to employees who stand up against discrimination?
a: A right to a pay rise
44548.e: A dismissal in response to a complaint can be challenged. The protection applies during the proceedings and for six months afterwards.
44548.m: Anyone who stands up against discrimination is protected from retaliatory dismissal.

44549.q: Which 1995 Council of Europe convention protects national minorities?
a: Framework Convention for the Protection of National Minorities
44549.e: The Framework Convention obliges states to protect the language, culture and identity of national minorities. Switzerland ratified it in 1998.
44549.m: The Council of Europe's Framework Convention protects national minorities.

44550.q: Which canton was created in 1979 partly to protect a French-speaking minority in the canton of Bern?
44550.e: The French-speaking, mostly Catholic people of the northern Jura felt disadvantaged in the canton of Bern. After several votes, the canton of Jura was founded in 1979.
44550.m: The canton of Jura is an example of resolving a minority conflict.

44551.q: Which language is especially protected in Switzerland by the European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages?
44551.e: Under this charter Switzerland mainly protects Romansh and Italian, which are minority languages in the country.
44551.m: The language charter helps to preserve Romansh.

44552.q: Since which year has Romansh been a national language of Switzerland?
44552.e: In the referendum of 1938 Romansh became the fourth national language. In 1996 it also became a partial official language of the Confederation.
44552.m: Romansh has been a national language since 1938.

44553.q: Which right does the UN Covenant on Civil and Political Rights guarantee to members of minorities?
a: To enjoy their own culture, religion and language
To have a fixed seat in parliament
44553.e: Art. 27 of the UN Covenant protects members of ethnic, religious or linguistic minorities. Switzerland joined the Covenant in 1992.
44553.m: The UN Covenant protects the culture, religion and language of minorities.

44554.q: Which element of Swiss democracy protects small cantons from being outvoted by populous cantons?
44554.e: Constitutional amendments need a majority of the cantons as well as a majority of the people. This gives small cantons more weight.
44554.m: The majority of the cantons gives small cantons a strong voice.

44555.q: Which principle in Art. 70 of the Federal Constitution protects the traditional language areas?
44555.e: The cantons respect the traditional linguistic make-up of areas and take account of long-established linguistic minorities.
44555.m: The territoriality principle preserves the traditional language areas.

44556.q: Which fundamental right of the Federal Constitution includes protection against misuse of personal data?
44556.e: The Federal Constitution protects privacy in Article 13. This expressly includes the right to protection against misuse of personal data.
44556.m: Data protection is part of the fundamental right to privacy.

44557.q: Since when has the EU General Data Protection Regulation applied?
44557.e: The GDPR has applied since 25 May 2018. It also affects Swiss companies that offer goods or services to people in the EU.
44557.m: The GDPR has effects beyond the borders of the EU.

44558.q: Which principle requires data protection to be planned in from the start when software is developed?
44558.e: The principle is known in English as “privacy by design”. Systems should be built from the start so that they comply with data protection rules.
44558.m: Data protection should be considered right from when software is built.

44559.q: What must a company do if a data security breach is likely to mean a high risk for the people affected?
a: Report it quickly to the supervisory authority
44559.e: The Data Protection Act requires a report to the responsible federal authority as quickly as possible. In some cases the people affected must also be informed.
44559.m: Serious data breaches must be reported to the authorities.

44560.q: Which term describes the right to decide for yourself about revealing and using your own data?
44560.e: The term comes from the German census ruling of 1983 and also shapes Swiss case law.
44560.m: Every person should be able to decide about their own data.

44561.q: Which right lets you find out from a company what data it has stored about you?
44561.e: Every person can ask the controller whether and which personal data about them are being processed. The information is usually free of charge.
44561.m: With the right of access you find out what is stored about you.

44562.q: What must a company produce before processing data that is likely to pose a high risk for the people affected?
44562.e: The impact assessment describes the planned processing, evaluates the risks and sets out protective measures.
44562.m: Risky data processing must be checked for its consequences beforehand.

44563.q: In Switzerland, who is usually fined for breaking the Data Protection Act?
44563.e: Unlike in the EU, fines in Switzerland are basically aimed at the responsible individual. They can be up to 250,000 francs.
44563.m: In Switzerland data protection breaches can lead to personal fines.

44564.q: Which term did the Society for the German Language choose as its word of the year in 2016?
44564.e: “Postfaktisch” describes an attitude in which feelings count for more than verifiable facts. In the same year Oxford Dictionaries chose “post-truth” as the English word of the year.
44564.m: In post-factual debate, feelings often count for more than facts.

44565.q: What did a much-discussed 2018 MIT study (in the journal “Science”) find about the spread of false news on Twitter?
a: False news spread faster than true news
True news spread faster than false news
False news was hardly ever shared
44565.e: The researchers led by Soroush Vosoughi found that false news was shared further, faster and more deeply than true news. Among the reasons they name its novelty and the strong feelings it triggers.
44565.m: False news often spreads faster than the truth.

a: Preparing people in advance against manipulation tricks
44566.e: Prebunking is based on inoculation theory: people who know manipulation techniques in advance fall for them less often. Debunking, by contrast, disproves a false claim only afterwards.
44566.m: Prebunking protects against manipulation before it takes effect.

44567.q: What are video or audio recordings called that have been faked with artificial intelligence so that they look or sound real?
44567.e: Deepfakes are made with machine learning methods and can make people say or do things that never happened. They are seen as a growing danger for political communication.
44567.m: Deepfakes are images, videos or audio recordings faked with AI.

44568.q: Which strategy do fact-checkers recommend for quickly assessing an unknown website?
a: Only reading the site's legal notice
44568.e: In lateral reading you leave the site and check in other sources who is behind it and what others say about it. Studies show that professional fact-checkers reach reliable judgements faster this way.
44568.m: To check a source, you should also read about it in other sources.

44569.q: What did the World Health Organization (WHO) call the flood of partly false information about Covid-19 in 2020?
44569.e: The term “infodemic” combines information and epidemic. It describes an excess of information that makes it hard to find reliable guidance.
44569.m: In an infodemic it is hard to find reliable information.

44570.q: Which word was chosen in Germany in 2014 as the “non-word of the year” because it defames the media wholesale?
44570.e: The jury criticised “Lügenpresse” for branding all media as controlled and lying. The term had already been used as a propaganda term in the Nazi era.
44570.m: The word “Lügenpresse” defames the media wholesale.

44571.q: Who coined the term “filter bubble” in 2011 with his book of the same name?
44571.e: In 2011 the US internet activist Eli Pariser described how algorithms mainly show users content that matches their previous preferences. This could shield them from other points of view.
44571.m: Eli Pariser made the term filter bubble well known.

44572.q: What mainly causes a filter bubble?
44572.e: Platforms and search engines analyse clicks, likes and time spent and show similar content. This tailors the selection unnoticed, without the person consciously deciding it.
44572.m: Filter bubbles are created by algorithms that personalise content.

44573.q: Which example did Eli Pariser use to illustrate filter bubbles?
a: Different Google results for the same search term
The same front pages in all newspapers
44573.e: Pariser had friends search for the same term and found that they got very different results. Google had personalised search for all users since 2009.
44573.m: Personalised search engines do not show everyone the same results.

44574.q: What is the main difference between a filter bubble and an echo chamber?
a: The filter bubble is caused mainly by algorithms
The echo chamber is caused only by algorithms
Both terms mean exactly the same
The filter bubble exists only on television
44574.e: The filter bubble stresses the invisible pre-selection by software. With the echo chamber the focus is on people surrounding themselves with like-minded others and reinforcing each other.
44574.m: The filter bubble is mainly the work of algorithms.

44575.q: What do many empirical studies show about the filter bubble theory?
a: The effect is usually weaker than feared
The effect has been shown to be very strong everywhere
Filter bubbles exist only among older people
44575.e: Researchers such as Axel Bruns conclude that most people do come across differing opinions online. Their own choices and social circle often have a stronger effect than the algorithm.
44575.m: Research gives less support for the filter bubble than is often claimed.

44576.q: What goal are the recommendation algorithms of big platforms typically optimised for?
a: The longest possible time spent using them
44576.e: Platforms earn money mainly through advertising and therefore want to hold attention. Content that triggers interaction is shown more often, which can encourage one-sidedness.
44576.m: Recommendation algorithms aim mainly to hold attention.

44577.q: What does the EU Digital Services Act (DSA) require of very large platforms regarding recommendation systems?
44577.e: Very large online platforms must offer at least one version of their recommendation system that is not based on personal profiling. This is meant to let users switch off personalisation.
44577.m: The DSA requires a recommendation option without personal profiling.

44578.q: Which personal step is most likely to help you get out of a filter bubble?
a: Deliberately using a variety of sources
44578.e: Anyone who deliberately reads media with different viewpoints widens their own information base. Likes and notifications, by contrast, tend to increase personalisation.
44578.m: A variety of sources widens your view beyond the filter bubble.

44579.q: Who described the danger of digital echo chambers as early as 2001 in the book “Republic.com”?
44579.e: The US legal scholar Cass Sunstein warned that people on the internet could select their information so strongly themselves that they would only hear like-minded people. He saw this as a danger for democratic debate.
44579.m: Cass Sunstein warned early about echo chambers on the internet.

44580.q: Which psychological effect strengthens echo chambers because people prefer information that confirms their views?
44580.e: With confirmation bias, people mainly seek out, notice and remember information that supports their opinion. Echo chambers feed this effect particularly well.
44580.m: Confirmation bias makes us notice confirming information more readily.

44581.q: What does “group polarisation” mean in connection with echo chambers?
a: Groups hold more extreme positions after discussion
Groups always split into two halves
Groups always agree on the middle
Groups break up after an argument
44581.e: When like-minded people discuss with each other, the group's opinion often shifts further in its original direction. Counter-arguments are missing, and they reinforce each other.
44581.m: Among like-minded people, opinions often become more extreme.

44582.q: What is the tendency to connect mainly with people who are similar to you called?
44582.e: Homophily is a sociological term along the lines of “birds of a feather flock together”. In social networks it helps echo chambers to form.
44582.m: Homophily means that similar people like to stick together.

44583.q: Which theory by Leon Festinger (1957) explains why people tend to avoid contradictory information?
a: Theory of the spiral of silence
44583.e: Contradictory information creates an unpleasant feeling of tension. To avoid it, people tend to choose content that fits their beliefs.
44583.m: Cognitive dissonance is an unpleasant inner contradiction.

44584.q: Why are echo chambers seen as a risk for democracy?
a: They make the exchange of arguments harder
44584.e: Democracy depends on different points of view meeting and compromises being sought. Anyone who only hears confirmation understands people who think differently less well, which increases polarisation.
44584.m: Democracy needs an exchange of different opinions.

44585.q: What is a typical feature of an echo chamber in a chat group?
a: Dissenting voices are put down or missing
All members know each other personally
44585.e: In echo chambers the same messages are repeated again and again, while disagreement hardly appears or is put down. This makes your own views seem like everyone's opinion.
44585.m: In an echo chamber you mainly hear the echo of your own opinion.

44586.q: Which St Petersburg organisation became known as a “troll factory” because of its interference in the 2016 US election?
44586.e: The Internet Research Agency ran many fake accounts to influence moods in the USA. A report by Special Counsel Robert Mueller described its activities in detail.
44586.m: Troll factories control many fake accounts at the same time.

44587.q: What is it called when a broad citizens' movement is faked but is in fact controlled from above?
44587.e: The term comes from the artificial turf brand AstroTurf and plays on “grassroots”. Social bots and fake accounts are often used for it.
44587.m: Astroturfing only pretends to be a grassroots movement.

44588.q: Which feature of an account most suggests that it is a social bot?
a: Very many posts around the clock
A few followers from the same town
44588.e: People sleep and post irregularly, but bots can publish hundreds of posts a day without a break. Other signs are new accounts, generic names and repeated texts.
44588.m: Non-stop posting is a sign of a bot.

44589.q: What is a “sock puppet” on social media?
a: A second account that pretends to be someone else
An account without a profile picture
44589.e: With sock puppets, people can create seemingly independent voices that support their own position. When many such accounts are automated, they are called bots.
44589.m: Sock puppets are disguised accounts with a false identity.

44590.q: Which freely available tool from Indiana University estimates whether an account on X (Twitter) is a bot?
44590.e: Botometer analyses features such as activity, network and language and calculates a probability. Such scores are estimates and can be wrong.
44590.m: Bot detection only gives probabilities, not certainty.

44591.q: How can social bots distort public perception of a topic?
a: By artificially pushing hashtags into the trends
44591.e: Many coordinated accounts can share a topic on a massive scale in a short time. This makes it seem more important or controversial than it really is among the public.
44591.m: Bots can artificially inflate the importance of a topic.

44592.q: Which test by Alan Turing (1950) checks whether a machine can be told apart from a human in conversation?
44592.e: Turing suggested that a machine could be considered “thinking” if a person in a text conversation cannot tell whether they are talking to a human or a machine. Modern chatbots make it harder to tell bots and humans apart.
44592.m: The Turing test asks whether machines can communicate like humans.

44593.q: What is meant by framing in political communication?
a: Placing a topic within a frame of interpretation
44593.e: In framing, certain aspects of a topic are highlighted and others left out. This influences how the audience understands and judges the topic.
44593.m: A frame is a frame of interpretation that steers perception.

44594.q: Which sociologist laid a foundation for framing research in 1974 with “Frame Analysis”?
44594.e: Erving Goffman studied how people interpret everyday situations with the help of frames. Communication science later applied the approach to media and politics.
44594.m: Erving Goffman is regarded as the founder of frame analysis.

44595.q: Which four functions of a frame did Robert Entman distinguish in 1993?
44595.e: According to Entman, a frame defines a problem, names causes, makes a moral judgement and recommends an action. These elements can be found in media texts.
44595.m: A frame includes a problem, a cause, a judgement and a proposed solution.

44596.q: Which famous experiment by Tversky and Kahneman (1981) showed framing effects with equivalent wordings?
44596.e: Participants chose different programmes depending on whether the wording was a gain (“200 will be saved”) or a loss (“400 will die”), even though the outcomes were the same. This is called equivalence framing.
44596.m: The same facts can have a different effect depending on the wording.

44597.q: Which book by the linguist George Lakoff made framing in politics popular in 2004?
44597.e: Lakoff showed that just repeating an opponent's term activates its frame. Anyone who denies the elephant still thinks of it.
44597.m: Even denying a term activates its frame.

44598.q: Which frame is contained in the expression “tax burden”?
a: Taxes as a contribution to the community
44598.e: The word “burden” presents taxes as something heavy from which people need relief. Other terms such as “tax contribution” stress the shared benefit instead.
44598.m: Even a single word can set a political frame.

44599.q: Why is talking about a “wave of refugees” seen as framing?
a: It presents people as a force of nature
It is a technical term of international law
44599.e: The metaphor of the wave calls up images of threat and loss of control. The refugees appear as a mass instead of as individual people.
44599.m: Metaphors such as wave or flood shape how migration is perceived.

44600.q: On the subject of video surveillance, one party talks only about security and the other only about freedom. What is this kind of framing called?
44600.e: In emphasis framing, different aspects of content are put in the foreground. In equivalence framing the content stays the same and only the wording changes.
44600.m: Emphasis framing puts certain aspects in the foreground.

44601.q: What is the core idea of the agenda-setting approach?
a: The media influence what people think about
The media decide exactly what people think
The media have no effect at all
44601.e: The media cannot directly dictate opinions, but they decide which topics are seen as important. A lot of coverage makes a topic significant for the audience.
44601.m: The media help decide which topics we consider important.

44602.q: Why is agenda setting important in a referendum campaign?
a: Whoever shapes the dominant topic steers voters' attention
Because the media decide the result of the vote
Because only topics on the agenda may be voted on
Because the Federal Council sets the media's agenda
44602.e: The media do not dictate opinions, but they help decide which topics are seen as important. Whoever puts a topic in the foreground influences what is discussed before the vote.
44602.m: The media help decide which topics we consider important.

44603.q: Which example fits agenda setting best?
a: After many reports on the housing shortage, more people think the issue is urgent
A newspaper tells people how they must vote
A channel shows nothing but sport
44603.e: Frequent coverage makes a topic more important for the audience. What people think about the topic is not yet decided by this.
44603.m: A lot of coverage makes a topic significant.

44604.e: Journalists act as “gatekeepers” and decide which reports get through. In 1950 David Manning White studied such a “Mr. Gates” in a newspaper office.
44604.m: Gatekeepers decide which news is published.

44605.q: Which theory by Galtung and Ruge (1965) explains which events become news?
44605.e: According to news value theory, events with factors such as proximity, prominence, negativity or surprise have a better chance of being reported. These factors shape the media agenda.
44605.m: News factors help decide what becomes news.

44606.q: What does “priming” mean in media effects research?
a: Topics in the spotlight become the yardstick for judgements
The first report in a programme
44606.e: When the media strongly emphasise a topic, people tend to judge politicians by how they handle that topic. Priming is seen as a follow-on effect of agenda setting.
44606.m: Priming makes topics in the spotlight the yardstick for political judgements.

a: Media take up topics from other media
Politicians set topics in the media
Readers write letters to the editor
44607.e: Leading media such as big newspapers or news agencies often set topics that other media then take up. This creates a similar agenda of topics across many media.
44607.m: The media often take over the topics of leading media.

44608.q: What does “framing” mean in media coverage?
a: How a topic is presented and put into context
How often a topic is mentioned
44608.e: Whether you speak of “tax relief” or a “tax giveaway”, for example, frames the same topic differently. Framing stresses certain aspects and so influences how it is judged.
44608.m: Framing decides in which light a topic appears.

44609.q: In which year did Switzerland vote on the No Billag initiative?
44609.e: The popular initiative “Yes to abolishing radio and television licence fees” was put to the vote on 4 March 2018. It sparked one of the most intense media debates of recent years.
44609.m: The No Billag initiative was put to the vote in 2018.

44610.q: What percentage of voters rejected the No Billag initiative?
44610.e: About 2.1 million voters said no and only about 834,000 yes. So the rejection was very clear.
44610.m: The No Billag initiative was rejected with over 70 per cent voting no.

44611.q: How many cantons approved the No Billag initiative?
44611.e: All cantons rejected the initiative. The highest yes shares were in Schwyz and Schaffhausen, with just over 37 per cent.
44611.m: No canton approved the No Billag initiative.

44612.q: What did the No Billag initiative demand?
a: The abolition of radio and television licence fees
44612.e: The Confederation would no longer have been allowed to charge licence fees or subsidise radio and television stations. For the SRG this would have meant losing most of its income.
44612.m: The No Billag initiative wanted to abolish broadcasting fees completely.

44613.q: Where did the name “Billag” in the No Billag initiative come from?
a: From the former fee collection agency
From an abbreviation in the law
44613.e: Until the end of 2018 Billag AG collected the radio and television fees on behalf of the Confederation. In everyday speech its name stood for the fees themselves.
44613.m: Billag AG used to be responsible for collecting the fees.

44614.q: Which company would have lost most of its income if the No Billag initiative had been accepted?
44614.e: The SRG is financed mostly by the radio and television levy. The initiative was clearly rejected with about 72 per cent voting no, on a turnout of about 54 per cent.
44614.m: The SRG lives mainly on the radio and television levy.

44615.q: Which region of the country rejected the No Billag initiative especially clearly?
44615.e: In western Switzerland the no share was especially high, close to 80 per cent in Neuchâtel and Jura. In central and eastern Switzerland support was somewhat higher, for example in Schwyz and Schaffhausen.
44615.m: French-speaking Switzerland rejected the No Billag initiative especially clearly.

44616.q: How did the annual household levy for radio and television change in 2019, a year after the No Billag vote?
44616.e: In 2019 the amount fell to 365 francs per household. The new levy is charged regardless of devices.
44616.m: The household levy fell significantly in 2019.

44617.q: What does the SRG platform Play Suisse offer?
a: Swiss films and series from all language regions with subtitles
44617.e: Play Suisse is an SRG streaming platform with Swiss productions subtitled in several national languages. It is meant to encourage exchange between the language regions.
44617.m: Play Suisse connects the language regions with Swiss films and series.

44618.q: Which unit of the SRG produces programmes in Romansh?
44618.e: RTR stands for Radiotelevisiun Svizra Rumantscha. RSI broadcasts in Italian, RTS in French and SRF in German.
44618.m: RTR is the SRG's Romansh company.

44619.q: According to the Federal Constitution, what is part of the SRG's “public service”?
a: A contribution to education, culture and free opinion-forming
44619.e: Article 93 of the Federal Constitution requires radio and television to contribute to education, cultural development, free opinion-forming and entertainment. They must take account of the country's particular features and the needs of the cantons.
44619.m: The public service should serve all parts of the country and support opinion-forming.

44620.q: Which SRG service is aimed at Swiss people living abroad and an international audience?
44620.e: Swissinfo offers information from Switzerland in ten languages. It is part of the SRG's international mandate.
44620.m: Swissinfo informs the world about Switzerland.

44621.q: How much has the annual radio and television levy per private household been since 2021 (as of 2026)?
44621.e: The levy fell to 335 francs in 2021. The Federal Council has also decided on a gradual reduction to 312 francs from 2027 and 300 francs from 2029.
44621.m: Since 2021 a private household has paid 335 francs a year.

44622.q: Who has held the post of Director-General of the SRG since November 2024?
44622.e: Susanne Wille took over the leadership of the SRG from Gilles Marchand. Before that she had been head of culture at SRF and a member of its executive board from 2020.
44622.m: Susanne Wille has led the SRG since November 2024.

44623.q: Why does the SRG receive most of the levy, even though there are private broadcasters too?
a: It must serve all language regions equally
44623.e: The SRG must provide a comparable service in all four national languages. The smaller language regions receive more money than they pay in; local private broadcasters also get a share of the levy.
44623.m: The SRG provides all language regions with an equivalent service.

44624.q: With a random sample of 1,000 people and a share of 50 per cent, roughly how large is the margin of error (95 per cent confidence interval)?
44624.e: The margin of error is 1.96 times the square root of 0.5 times 0.5 divided by 1,000, which is about 0.031. That corresponds to about 3.1 percentage points.
44624.m: Even good polls have a statistical margin of error.

44625.q: How does the sampling error change if you multiply the number of people surveyed by four?
44625.e: The sampling error depends on the square root of the sample size. The square root of 4 is 2, so the error becomes half as big.
44625.m: To halve the error, you need four times as many people surveyed.

44626.q: Which magazine got its forecast for the 1936 US presidential election wrong despite more than two million replies?
44626.e: The Literary Digest predicted a win for Alf Landon, but Franklin D. Roosevelt won clearly. The people surveyed came mainly from wealthy groups, so the sample was biased.
44626.m: A large sample is of little use if it is not representative.

44627.q: What is a leading question in a survey?
a: A question that suggests a particular answer
A question with an open answer
A question at the end of the questionnaire
44627.e: Wordings such as “Don't you also think that ...” push respondents in one direction. Serious surveys therefore use questions that are as neutral as possible.
44627.m: Neutral questions are the basis of a serious survey.

44628.q: What is the effect called when undecided people join the side leading in the polls?
44628.e: With the bandwagon effect, people want to be on the winning side. The opposite effect, where the losing side gains support, is called the underdog effect.
44628.m: The bandwagon effect strengthens the side leading in the polls.

44629.q: Why is the raw data of a survey often “weighted”?
a: To reflect the make-up of the population
To reduce the number of questions
44629.e: If certain groups, such as young people, are under-represented in the sample, their answers are given more weight. This brings the sample closer to the known features of the whole population.
44629.m: Weighting evens out distortions in the sample.

44630.q: Why are online polls in which anyone can choose to click along not representative?
a: They have too many answer options
44630.e: In such polls it is mainly very interested or mobilised people who take part. Without random selection, no conclusions can be drawn about the whole population.
44630.m: Without random selection a survey is not representative.

44631.q: What is meant by civil society?
a: The area of voluntary organisations between the state, the market and the family
44631.e: Civil society includes clubs, associations, foundations, citizens' initiatives and non-governmental organisations. They act voluntarily and do not mainly pursue profit or state power.
44631.m: Civil society includes voluntary organisations outside the state and the market.

44632.q: Which French thinker praised the importance of voluntary associations in “Democracy in America” (1835)?
44632.e: Tocqueville observed that Americans formed associations for almost every cause. He saw this as a school of democracy.
44632.m: Tocqueville saw associations as a school of democracy.

44633.q: Which book by Robert Putnam (2000) describes the decline of social capital in the USA?
44633.e: Putnam showed that people still go bowling, but less often in clubs. As such networks decline, the trust that a democracy needs declines too.
44633.m: Social capital comes from trust and networks in society.

44634.q: What is needed in Switzerland to set up an association with a non-commercial purpose?
44634.e: Under Art. 60 of the Civil Code, an association comes into being as soon as the will to exist as a body is shown in written articles of association. Registration in the commercial register is usually not necessary.
44634.m: In Switzerland an association can easily be founded with articles of association.

44635.q: Through which procedure can civil society organisations in Switzerland comment on draft laws?
44635.e: In the consultation, cantons, parties, associations and anyone interested can submit their views on federal proposals. That way their knowledge feeds into lawmaking early.
44635.m: The consultation lets civil society organisations have their say too.

44636.q: Which popular initiative by a broad coalition of aid organisations failed in 2020 on the majority of the cantons despite a majority of the people?
44636.e: On 29 November 2020 the Responsible Business Initiative won about 50.7 per cent yes, but not the majority of the cantons. It was backed by more than a hundred civil society organisations.
44636.m: A popular initiative needs a majority of the people and of the cantons.

44637.q: Which Italian thinker shaped the idea of civil society as a place of struggle for cultural hegemony?
44637.e: Antonio Gramsci saw civil society as the space in which groups struggle for consent and the power to define meaning. His concept of hegemony still has an impact in the social sciences today.
44637.m: Gramsci linked civil society with the struggle over who defines meaning.

44638.q: Which US writer wrote the 1849 essay that later became famous under the title “Civil Disobedience”?
44638.e: Thoreau refused to pay taxes in protest against slavery and the war against Mexico, and spent a night in prison as a result. His essay, originally “Resistance to Civil Government”, later influenced Gandhi and Martin Luther King.
44638.m: Thoreau is regarded as a pioneer of civil disobedience.

44639.q: Which feature belongs to civil disobedience?
44639.e: Civil disobedience is a deliberate, public and non-violent breaking of rules for reasons of conscience. It often includes being prepared to accept the legal consequences.
44639.m: Civil disobedience breaks rules deliberately, publicly and non-violently.

44640.q: With which protest did Mahatma Gandhi defy a British monopoly in 1930?
44640.e: Gandhi marched about 385 kilometres to the sea and made salt there, which broke the British salt law. Thousands followed his example.
44640.m: The Salt March became a symbol of non-violent resistance.

44641.q: Which action by Rosa Parks in Montgomery in 1955 is regarded as an act of civil disobedience?
a: She did not give up her seat on the bus
44641.e: Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat to a white passenger and was arrested. This led to the Montgomery bus boycott.
44641.m: Rosa Parks became a symbol of the civil rights movement.

44642.q: In which 1963 text did Martin Luther King justify breaking unjust laws?
44642.e: King wrote the letter in prison and in it distinguished just from unjust laws. Anyone who openly breaks an unjust law and accepts the punishment shows the highest respect for the law.
44642.m: Martin Luther King distinguished just and unjust laws.

44643.q: Which philosopher defined civil disobedience in 1971 in “A Theory of Justice”?
44643.e: Rawls described civil disobedience as a public, non-violent, conscientious but illegal act aimed at changing a law or policy. His definition is still influential today.
44643.m: John Rawls provided an influential definition of civil disobedience.

44644.q: Which site did anti-nuclear protesters occupy for eleven weeks in Switzerland in 1975?
a: The nuclear power plant site at Kaiseraugst
44644.e: The occupation of Kaiseraugst is regarded as an important event in the Swiss anti-nuclear movement. The planned nuclear power plant was never built.
44644.m: The occupation of Kaiseraugst shaped the Swiss anti-nuclear movement.

44645.q: How did the Federal Supreme Court decide in 2021 in the case of the climate activists who had played tennis in a bank branch in Lausanne in 2018?
a: It acquitted them on grounds of necessity
It referred the case to the UN
44645.e: The Lausanne district court had at first acquitted the activists, citing a state of necessity. But the cantonal court and finally the Federal Supreme Court found there was no justifying necessity.
44645.m: Under Swiss law, good intentions do not justify every breach of the rules.

44646.q: Who started the “school strike for climate” outside the Swedish parliament in August 2018?
44646.e: Greta Thunberg, then 15, sat with a sign outside the parliament in Stockholm. This grew into the worldwide Fridays for Future movement.
44646.m: Greta Thunberg's school strike set off a worldwide movement.

44647.q: What is a central demand of Climate Strike Switzerland?
a: Net zero emissions within the country by 2030
Net zero by 2050 with offsetting abroad
A ban on all petrol cars by 2025
44647.e: The movement demands that Switzerland cut its greenhouse gas emissions within the country to net zero by 2030, without offsetting abroad. It also calls for climate justice.
44647.m: Climate Strike demands net zero by 2030.

44648.q: Which law did Swiss voters approve on 18 June 2023 with about 59 per cent voting yes?
44648.e: The law was the indirect counter-proposal to the Glacier Initiative. It sets the goal of net zero by 2050.
44648.m: Switzerland aims to be climate-neutral by 2050.

44649.q: What was the result of the vote on the revised CO2 Act on 13 June 2021?
a: It was never put to the vote
44649.e: About 51.6 per cent of voters said no. For the climate movement this was a setback, after it had mobilised many people in 2019.
44649.m: The CO2 Act narrowly failed at the ballot box in 2021.

44650.q: Which action by climate activists in Bern in September 2020 led to police clearing the area?
a: The occupation of the Federal Square
The occupation of the Federal Supreme Court
The closure of the main station
44650.e: Under the name “Rise up for Change”, activists occupied the Federal Square during the autumn session. Because rallies there are not permitted during the session, the police cleared the camp.
44650.m: During the session, rallies on the Federal Square are heavily restricted.

44651.q: What is the worldwide movement called that grew out of the school strikes for climate?
44651.e: Fridays for Future organises school strikes and demonstrations, mostly on Fridays. Extinction Rebellion is a different group that relies more on civil disobedience.
44651.m: Fridays for Future grew out of the school strikes for climate.

44652.q: What is the main legal question raised by school strikes?
a: Whether staying away counts as an unexcused absence
Whether the Federal Council must agree
44652.e: Taking part in the strike during school hours falls under the cantonal rules on absences. Schools dealt with it in different ways, from penalties to tolerating it.
44652.m: Legally, school strikes are mainly a question of absences.

44653.q: Which gatherings are not protected by freedom of assembly?
a: Small gatherings of a few people
44653.e: Fundamental and human rights expressly protect only peaceful gatherings. Anyone who uses violence cannot rely on freedom of assembly.
44653.m: Only peaceful gatherings are protected by freedom of assembly.

44654.q: Why may authorities require a permit for a demonstration on public land?
a: Because it uses streets and squares more than usual
Because demonstrations are banned in principle
Because every rally counts as advertising
44654.e: A demonstration restricts others more than the normal use of streets and squares. Lawyers speak of increased common use, for which a permit with conditions may be required.
44654.m: Demonstrations use public land beyond the usual level.

44655.q: In Switzerland, who is usually responsible for granting permits for demonstrations?
44655.e: The use of public land and police powers lie with the cantons and municipalities. In cities such as Zurich or Bern, the city administration usually issues the permit.
44655.m: Demonstrations are usually permitted by municipalities or cantons.

44656.q: What entitlement does the Federal Supreme Court recognise for rallies on public land?
a: A conditional right to a permit
44656.e: Authorities must consider the importance of fundamental rights in their decision and may not ban a rally without weighty reasons. But conditions on route, time or safety are possible.
44656.m: Rallies may not be banned without weighty reasons.

44657.q: What does the principle of proportionality require before a demonstration is banned?
a: That milder means such as conditions are not enough
That at least 1,000 people take part
44657.e: A restriction must be suitable, necessary and reasonable. A ban is only allowed if conditions, for example on route or time, cannot avert the danger.
44657.m: A ban is only the last resort.

44658.q: Besides the Federal Constitution, which international agreement protects freedom of assembly in Switzerland?
a: The European Convention on Human Rights
44658.e: Art. 11 ECHR guarantees peaceful assembly and the right to form associations. Switzerland ratified the ECHR in 1974.
44658.m: The ECHR also protects peaceful gatherings.

a: A rally as an immediate reaction with no time to apply
A permitted demo with long planning
A demonstration only on the internet
44659.e: Spontaneous demonstrations react at short notice to an event, so no normal permit procedure is possible. If they are peaceful, authorities should usually tolerate them.
44659.m: Spontaneous rallies react immediately to an event.

44660.q: Which condition may authorities typically set for a permitted demonstration?
a: Censor the content of the speeches
44660.e: Authorities can regulate place, time, route and safety measures to protect traffic and other people affected. They may not dictate the content of what is expressed.
44660.m: Authorities regulate how a demonstration happens, not its message.

44661.q: Which organisation publishes the well-known Democracy Index, which has appeared since 2006?
44661.e: The Democracy Index is produced by the Economist Intelligence Unit, a research division of the Economist Group. The first edition appeared in 2006.
44661.m: The Democracy Index is produced by the Economist Intelligence Unit.

44662.q: On what scale does the Economist's Democracy Index rate countries?
44662.e: Each country gets an overall score between 0 and 10. It is the average of the scores in five categories.
44662.m: The Democracy Index gives scores from 0 to 10.

44663.q: Into how many types of regime does the Democracy Index divide countries?
44663.e: It distinguishes full democracies, flawed democracies, hybrid regimes and authoritarian regimes.
44663.m: The Democracy Index has four types of regime.

44664.q: From what overall score is a country considered a full democracy in the Democracy Index?
44664.e: Countries with more than 8 out of 10 points count as full democracies. Between 6 and 8 points they are called flawed democracies.
44664.m: A full democracy needs more than 8 points in the Democracy Index.

44665.q: In the Democracy Index, what is the type of regime with a score between 4 and 6 points called?
44665.e: Hybrid regimes score between 4 and 6 points. They combine democratic elements such as elections with authoritarian features such as pressure on the media and courts.
44665.m: Hybrid regimes mix democratic and authoritarian features.

44666.q: Which of the following categories is one of the five areas of the Democracy Index?
44666.e: The five categories are electoral process and pluralism, functioning of government, political participation, political culture and civil liberties.
44666.m: Political culture is one of the five categories of the Democracy Index.

44667.q: Which country has regularly come first in the Democracy Index for many years?
44667.e: Norway has led the Democracy Index for more than a decade. It achieves top scores in almost all categories.
44667.m: Norway is usually at the top of the Democracy Index.

44668.q: How did the Democracy Index classify the USA from the edition for 2016 onwards?
44668.e: In 2016 the USA fell just below 8 points. The Economist Intelligence Unit mainly gave falling trust in institutions as the reason.
44668.m: Since 2016 the USA has been a flawed democracy in the Democracy Index.

44669.q: Roughly how many states and territories does the Economist's Democracy Index examine?
44669.e: The index rates 165 independent states and two territories. Microstates such as Monaco or Liechtenstein are missing.
44669.m: The Democracy Index compares about 167 states and territories.

44670.q: In which city does the organisation Freedom House have its headquarters?
44670.e: Freedom House is a non-governmental organisation based in Washington, D.C. It was founded in New York in 1941.
44670.m: Freedom House is based in Washington, D.C.

44671.q: What is Freedom House's main annual report on the state of freedom worldwide called?
44671.e: The report “Freedom in the World” has appeared every year since the 1970s. It rates political rights and civil liberties in almost all countries.
44671.m: Freedom House's main report is called “Freedom in the World”.

44672.q: Into which three groups does Freedom House divide countries?
44672.e: Depending on its score, a country counts as “Free”, “Partly Free” or “Not Free”. The basis is political rights and civil liberties.
44672.m: Freedom House distinguishes free, partly free and not free countries.

44673.q: Which two main areas does Freedom House assess in “Freedom in the World”?
44673.e: There are up to 40 points for political rights and up to 60 points for civil liberties. Together that makes a maximum of 100 points.
44673.m: Freedom House measures political rights and civil liberties.

44674.q: What is the maximum number of points a country can reach in “Freedom in the World”?
44674.e: A maximum of 40 points for political rights and 60 points for civil liberties makes 100 points. Switzerland regularly scores over 90 points.
44674.m: A country can reach at most 100 points with Freedom House.

44675.q: Which then First Lady of the USA was one of the founding figures of Freedom House?
44675.e: In 1941 Eleanor Roosevelt and the politician Wendell Willkie were among the honorary chairs. At that time the organisation was meant to rally opposition to fascism.
44675.m: Eleanor Roosevelt helped found Freedom House in 1941.

44676.q: Which trend has Freedom House reported in its annual reports for about two decades?
a: A steady increase in free countries
44676.e: Since the mid-2000s, scores have got worse in more countries each year than have improved. Freedom House speaks of a continuing decline in freedom.
44676.m: For about 20 years Freedom House has measured a decline in freedom worldwide.

44677.q: Which Freedom House report examines freedom on the internet?
44677.e: “Freedom on the Net” assesses obstacles to access, censorship and surveillance on the internet. “Nations in Transit”, by contrast, covers Eastern Europe and Central Asia.
44677.m: The report “Freedom on the Net” measures internet freedom.

44678.q: Which writer made the term “illiberal democracy” well known in 1997 with an essay in “Foreign Affairs”?
44678.e: In 1997 Fareed Zakaria described states with free elections but without protection of fundamental rights and the rule of law. His essay was called “The Rise of Illiberal Democracy”.
44678.m: Fareed Zakaria coined the term illiberal democracy in 1997.

a: Elections without effective protection of fundamental rights
Rule by a king with a constitution
44679.e: In an illiberal democracy elections take place. But the separation of powers, media freedom and minority rights are restricted.
44679.m: An illiberal democracy has elections but protects freedoms poorly.

44680.q: Which head of government openly committed himself in a 2014 speech to building an “illiberal state”?
44680.e: The Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán said this in 2014 in Băile Tușnad in Romania. The speech is regarded as a key text of Hungary's illiberal turn.
44680.m: In 2014 Viktor Orbán spoke openly of the illiberal state.

44681.q: Compared with liberal democracy, which element is an illiberal democracy mainly missing?
44681.e: Liberal democracy combines majority rule with the rule of law and fundamental rights. In illiberal democracies it is above all the independent judiciary that is weakened.
44681.m: Without an independent rule of law, a democracy becomes illiberal.

44682.q: What do the political scientists Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way call regimes with real but unfair elections?
44682.e: In competitive authoritarianism the opposition may stand. But the government gives itself big advantages through control of the media and pressure on the courts.
44682.m: In competitive authoritarianism elections are real but not fair.

44683.q: Which term describes rule by a majority that ignores the rights of minorities?
44683.e: The expression was used by Alexis de Tocqueville and John Stuart Mill, among others. Illiberal governments often invoke the will of the majority to cut back minority rights.
44683.m: The tyranny of the majority threatens the rights of minorities.

44684.q: Which method do illiberal governments often use to weaken critical media?
a: Takeover by owners close to the government
44684.e: In Hungary, businesspeople close to the government bought up many media outlets and combined them in a foundation in 2018. This creates influence without open censorship.
44684.m: Illiberal governments often control the media through friendly owners.

44685.q: Which procedure did the EU Parliament start against Hungary in 2018 because of a threat to EU values?
44685.e: In 2018 the European Parliament voted for a procedure under Article 7 of the EU Treaty. It concerns the risk of serious breaches of the Union's values.
44685.m: Since 2018 an Article 7 procedure has been under way against Hungary.

44686.q: Which party pushed through the controversial judicial reform in Poland from 2015?
44686.e: The national conservative PiS governed with an absolute majority from 2015 to 2023. It reshaped the Constitutional Tribunal, the National Council of the Judiciary and the Supreme Court.
44686.m: From 2015 the PiS party drove the restructuring of the Polish judiciary.

44687.q: Which court was at the centre of the first Polish constitutional crisis from 2015?
44687.e: The PiS majority refused to recognise judges elected by the previous parliament and installed its own judges. As a result the Constitutional Tribunal lost its role as an independent check.
44687.m: The Polish constitutional crisis began in 2015 at the Constitutional Tribunal.

44688.q: Which procedure did the EU Commission start against Poland in December 2017, for the first time in its history?
a: A procedure under Article 7 of the EU Treaty
A procedure to expel it from the EU
44688.e: The Commission saw the rule of law in Poland as seriously threatened. It was the first time it had triggered this procedure; it closed it again in 2024.
44688.m: In 2017 an Article 7 procedure was started for the first time, against Poland.

44689.q: Which new chamber of Poland's Supreme Court was particularly controversial?
44689.e: The Disciplinary Chamber, created in 2018, could punish judges. The European Court of Justice found its independence was not guaranteed; it was dissolved in 2022.
44689.m: The Disciplinary Chamber threatened the independence of Polish judges.

44690.q: How high was the daily penalty imposed on Poland by the European Court of Justice in 2021?
44690.e: Because Poland did not stop the Disciplinary Chamber, the ECJ imposed a penalty of 1 million euros per day in October 2021. It was later halved.
44690.m: The ECJ imposed a penalty of one million euros a day on Poland.

44691.q: Which body that proposes judges was restructured in 2017 so that parliament elects its judge members?
a: The National Council of the Judiciary (KRS)
44691.e: Until 2017 judges elected the judge members of the National Council of the Judiciary themselves. After that the Sejm chose them, which strengthened the governing majority.
44691.m: From 2017 the Sejm elected the judges on Poland's National Council of the Judiciary.

44692.q: Who was both Minister of Justice and Prosecutor General in Poland from 2016?
44692.e: In 2016 the offices of Minister of Justice and Prosecutor General were merged. This gave Zbigniew Ziobro great influence over criminal prosecution.
44692.m: Zbigniew Ziobro combined the justice ministry and the prosecution service in one person.

44693.q: What did critics call the 2020 Polish law that made it harder for judges to criticise the judicial reform?
44693.e: The law threatened judges with sanctions if they questioned the legitimacy of appointed judges. Critics therefore called it a muzzle law.
44693.m: Poland's 2020 muzzle law was meant to intimidate critical judges.

44694.q: On which date did supporters of Donald Trump storm the Capitol in Washington?
44694.e: On 6 January 2021 thousands forced their way into the Capitol. There, Congress was due to confirm Joe Biden's election victory.
44694.m: The storming of the Capitol happened on 6 January 2021.

44695.q: Which process in Congress did the attackers on 6 January 2021 want to prevent?
a: The certification of the electoral votes
The election of the Majority Leader
44695.e: After the presidential election, Congress counts the votes of the Electoral College. The session was interrupted and continued during the night.
44695.m: On 6 January 2021 Congress was due to confirm Biden's victory.

44696.q: Who, as Vice President, presided over the session to count the electoral votes on 6 January 2021?
44696.e: As President of the Senate, the Vice President presides over the count. Mike Pence refused to overturn the result in Trump's favour and was threatened by attackers.
44696.m: Mike Pence presided over the vote count on 6 January 2021.

44697.q: Under which slogan did Trump supporters spread the claim that the 2020 election had been stolen?
44697.e: “Stop the Steal” stood for the unproven claim of massive election fraud. Courts threw out most lawsuits against the election result.
44697.m: “Stop the Steal” was the slogan of the 2020 election fraud claim.

44698.q: What did the House of Representatives decide against Donald Trump on 13 January 2021?
44698.e: It was Trump's second impeachment. The Senate acquitted him in February 2021 because the necessary two-thirds majority was not reached.
44698.m: After the storming of the Capitol, Trump was impeached a second time.

44699.q: How many votes were cast in the Senate for convicting Trump in February 2021?
44699.e: 57 senators voted guilty, including 7 Republicans. A conviction would have needed 67 votes.
44699.m: In 2021 ten votes were missing for a conviction in the Senate.

44700.q: What did Donald Trump do on 20 January 2025 regarding those convicted over 6 January?
a: He set up a commission of inquiry
44700.e: On the first day of his second term, Trump pardoned about 1,500 people. For 14 others he commuted their sentences.
44700.m: In 2025 Trump pardoned most of those convicted over the storming of the Capitol.

44701.q: Which group in the House of Representatives investigated the events of 6 January from 2021 to 2022?
44701.e: The select committee held public hearings and presented a final report at the end of 2022. It also recommended criminal investigations against Trump.
44701.m: A select committee of the House of Representatives investigated 6 January.

44702.q: According to the well-known definition by political scientist Cas Mudde, which contrast is at the centre of populism?
a: The pure people against the corrupt elite
44702.e: Cas Mudde calls populism a thin ideology, because it can be combined with left-wing or right-wing ideas. At its core is the contrast between the people and the elite.
44702.m: For Cas Mudde, populism sets the people against the elite.

44703.q: What does the charge that populists are “anti-pluralist” mean?
a: They claim that they alone represent the true people
They want to abolish all taxes
44703.e: The political scientist Jan-Werner Müller stresses that populists claim to be the only ones representing the true people. People who think differently are then seen as illegitimate.
44703.m: Populists claim that they alone represent the people.

44704.q: In which country did the People's Party, an early populist movement, emerge in the 1890s?
44704.e: The People's Party mainly represented indebted farmers against banks and railway companies. Its supporters were called Populists.
44704.m: The first populist party emerged in the USA in the 1890s.

44705.q: Which contrast is typical of the rhetoric of left-wing populism?
a: The people against the economic elite
44705.e: Left-wing populism is directed mainly against banks, corporations and the rich. Right-wing populism, by contrast, often also excludes immigrants.
44705.m: Left-wing populism is directed mainly against economic elites.

44706.q: Which philosopher is the idea of a single “general will” (volonté générale) traced back to, which populists like to invoke?
44706.e: Rousseau described the volonté générale in “The Social Contract” (1762). Populists often claim to know this single will of the people.
44706.m: The idea of the general will comes from Jean-Jacques Rousseau.

44707.q: Which Spanish party is regarded as a well-known example of left-wing populism?
44707.e: Podemos emerged in 2014 from protests against austerity and sets the people against the elite. Its founders drew on the theories of Chantal Mouffe and Ernesto Laclau. Vox, by contrast, is right-wing populist.
44707.m: Podemos is an example of left-wing populism.

44708.q: What is the general criticism of established parties and institutions by populist movements called?
44708.e: Populists present themselves as outsiders against the political establishment. This includes parties, the media and often the courts too.
44708.m: Populism is marked by an anti-establishment attitude.

44709.q: Why are referendums often seen as especially important by populists?
a: They promise a direct expression of the will of the people
They strengthen the power of the courts
44709.e: Populists often demand more direct democracy because they set the will of the people against the elite. In Switzerland, by contrast, referendums have long been a fixed part of the system.
44709.m: Populists like to invoke referendums as an expression of the will of the people.

44710.q: Which word did the Society for the German Language choose as its word of the year in 1992?
44710.e: “Politikverdrossenheit” became word of the year in 1992. It describes citizens' growing distance from politics and politicians.
44710.m: “Politikverdrossenheit” was the German word of the year in 1992.

44711.q: Which sign is often seen as an indication of disenchantment with politics?
44711.e: If fewer and fewer people vote, this can point to disappointment with politics. But there are also other reasons, such as satisfaction or lack of time.
44711.m: Falling turnout can point to disenchantment with politics.

44712.q: Roughly what was the turnout in the 2023 Swiss National Council elections?
44712.e: According to the Federal Statistical Office, turnout in 2023 was 46.6 per cent. Since the 1970s it has mostly been below half.
44712.m: In the 2023 National Council elections just under half of those eligible voted.

44713.q: What is a form of disenchantment with politics called that is directed mainly against parties?
44713.e: Many people are interested in political issues but distrust the parties. This attitude is called disenchantment with parties.
44713.m: Disenchantment with parties is aimed at parties, not at politics as such.

44714.q: Which objection is often raised against the term “disenchantment with politics”?
a: Many people are not turned off politics, just disappointed with politicians
It is only used in Switzerland
44714.e: Researchers therefore prefer to speak of disenchantment with politicians or with institutions. Young people, for example, get involved in movements instead of parties.
44714.m: Behind disenchantment with politics there is often disappointment with politicians, not lack of interest.

44715.q: Which form of political participation has tended to increase among young people in recent decades?
a: Taking part in protest movements and petitions
44715.e: Young people take part more often in issue-based actions such as the climate strikes. Fixed party loyalties, by contrast, are declining.
44715.m: Today young people often get involved in movements rather than parties.

44716.q: What consequence can permanently low turnout have for democracy?
a: Those elected represent only a small part of the population
44716.e: If certain groups hardly vote, their interests are missing in parliament. This is then called a problem of representation.
44716.m: Low turnout weakens the representation of the population.

44717.q: Which Swiss canton is the only one that still has compulsory voting with a fine?
44717.e: Anyone in the canton of Schaffhausen who does not vote without an excuse pays a small fine. The canton therefore usually has the highest turnout in Switzerland.
44717.m: In the canton of Schaffhausen voting is compulsory.

44718.q: Which British social scientist coined the term “post-democracy”?
44718.e: Colin Crouch published the book “Post-Democracy” in 2004. It appeared in German in 2008 under the title “Postdemokratie”.
44718.m: Colin Crouch coined the term post-democracy.

44719.q: According to Colin Crouch, what formally remains in place in post-democracy?
44719.e: Elections still take place and governments can be voted out. But the election campaign becomes a spectacle steered by PR experts.
44719.m: In post-democracy elections remain but lose their meaning.

44720.q: According to Crouch, who has a big say in shaping policy behind the scenes in post-democracy?
44720.e: According to Crouch, elected governments and representatives of business interests increasingly negotiate policy among themselves. Citizens become passive spectators.
44720.m: In post-democracy, economic elites gain great influence.

44721.q: According to Colin Crouch, what does post-democracy resemble in some ways?
a: The people's assembly in ancient Athens
The planned economy of the Soviet Union
44721.e: Crouch describes democracy as a parabola: it rises, reaches a peak and falls again. In the end small elites again have a lot of influence, similar to before democracy.
44721.m: Crouch describes democracy as a parabola with a rise and a fall.

44722.q: When does Crouch see the high point of democracy in Western Europe and North America?
a: In the decades after the Second World War
After the fall of the Berlin Wall
44722.e: According to Crouch, mass parties, trade unions and the welfare state were strong at that time. Broad sections of the population could influence politics effectively.
44722.m: Crouch sees the high point of democracy in the post-war period.

44723.q: Which institution does Crouch see as central to power in post-democracy?
44723.e: Big corporations can put pressure on states by moving their locations. This increases their political weight compared with voters.
44723.m: For Crouch, the global company is the key institution of post-democracy.

44724.q: In 2011 Colin Crouch examined why neoliberal ideas survived a major crisis. Which crisis?
44724.e: In his book “The Strange Non-Death of Neoliberalism”, Crouch asked why these ideas continued to dominate after the 2008 financial crisis. The book builds on his analysis of post-democracy.
44724.m: Crouch asked why neoliberalism survived the 2008 financial crisis.

44725.q: According to Crouch's post-democracy theory, what role do citizens increasingly have?
44725.e: Citizens only react to the signals they are given in election campaigns. Real participation in shaping things hardly takes place.

a: Rule by experts instead of elected politicians
44726.e: In a technocracy, experts decide on the basis of specialist knowledge. Critics complain that they lack the democratic legitimacy of elections.

44727.q: Which economics professor led a government of experts in Italy from 2011 to 2013?
44727.e: During the euro crisis Mario Monti took charge of a cabinet of experts without party posts. He pushed through tough austerity measures.
44727.m: Mario Monti led a government of experts in Italy from 2011 to 2013.

44728.q: Which former President of the European Central Bank became Italian Prime Minister in 2021?
44728.e: Mario Draghi led a broad government from 2021 to 2022 that relied heavily on expertise. Before that he had headed the ECB from 2011 to 2019.
