44955.e: ICAO is a UN specialised agency. Its Council of 36 states adopts standards on things such as licences, air traffic control and accident investigation.
44955.m: ICAO sets the worldwide rules for civil aviation.

44956.q: Which spelling alphabet did ICAO lay down for radio communication?
44956.e: The ICAO alphabet has been in international use since the 1950s. Alfa is deliberately spelt with an f so that it is pronounced correctly everywhere.
44956.m: The ICAO alphabet begins with Alfa and Bravo.

44957.q: What is the name of the system adopted by ICAO in 2016 to offset CO2 emissions from international aviation?
44957.e: CORSIA requires airlines to offset increases in emissions on international flights through climate projects. It is the first global climate instrument for a whole economic sector.
44957.m: CORSIA is meant to offset the growth in aviation emissions.

44958.q: What are the technical rulebooks attached to the Chicago Convention called?
44958.e: The 19 annexes today contain standards and recommendations, for example on licences, air traffic control or accident investigation. Countries put them into national law.
44958.m: The annexes to the Chicago Convention contain the technical standards of aviation.

44959.q: What is the purpose of air accident investigations under ICAO rules?
44959.e: Annex 13 to the Chicago Convention states that investigations serve prevention, not the allocation of blame. In Switzerland, the STSB (SUST) is responsible for this.
44959.m: Air accidents are investigated to prevent future accidents.

44960.q: Which language must pilots and air traffic controllers master for international radio communication under ICAO rules?
44960.e: English is the language of international aviation radio. Since 2008, pilots and controllers have had to prove at least level 4 on the ICAO scale.
44960.m: English is compulsory in international aviation radio.

44961.q: What happens to a treaty between states that breaks a peremptory norm of international law (ius cogens)?
a: It is valid for only ten years
It must be confirmed by the people
It stays valid, but without penalties
44961.e: A treaty that breaks ius cogens is invalid from the start. This is laid down in the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties.
44961.m: A treaty that breaks ius cogens is void.

44962.q: May two states agree in a treaty not to respect the ban on torture?
a: No, peremptory international law cannot be set aside
Yes, but only during a war
Yes, if the UN Security Council agrees
44962.e: The ban on torture is part of ius cogens. Such norms apply to all states and cannot be overridden by any treaty.
44962.m: No treaty may depart from peremptory international law.

44963.q: Who must recognise a rule as a peremptory norm of international law (ius cogens) for it to count as one?
a: The international community of states as a whole
The International Court of Justice alone
44963.e: Under the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, a norm is peremptory if the international community of states as a whole recognises it. No single body can decide this on its own.
44963.m: Ius cogens rests on recognition by the whole community of states.

44964.q: Which of these norms is generally regarded as ius cogens?
44964.e: Like the bans on torture, genocide and aggression, the ban on slavery belongs to the recognised core of peremptory international law. Customs tariffs or visa rules, by contrast, can be freely negotiated.
44964.m: The ban on slavery is a peremptory norm of international law.

44965.q: Which ban did the International Court of Justice explicitly call ius cogens for the first time in 2006?
a: The ban on the death penalty
The ban on nuclear weapons tests
44965.e: In the case Congo v. Rwanda, the Court called the ban on genocide a peremptory norm. The death penalty, by contrast, is not generally banned under international law.
44965.m: The ban on genocide is part of peremptory international law.

44966.q: What happens in Switzerland if a popular initiative violates peremptory rules of international law?
a: The Federal Assembly declares it invalid
It is voted on only in the cantons
The Federal Supreme Court changes its text
It automatically lapses after five years
44966.e: Under Article 139 paragraph 3 of the Federal Constitution, the Federal Assembly declares a popular initiative wholly or partly invalid if it violates peremptory international law. This happened in 1996 with an asylum initiative because of the principle of non-refoulement.
44966.m: In Switzerland, popular initiatives must not violate peremptory international law.

44967.q: What does the Latin expression “erga omnes”, often found together with ius cogens in international law, mean?
44967.e: A state owes obligations erga omnes to the whole community of states, for example the ban on genocide. That is why all states may insist that they are respected.
44967.m: Obligations erga omnes apply towards all states.

44968.q: In which city was the 1969 Convention on the Law of Treaties, which first defined ius cogens, concluded?
44968.e: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties sets out how treaties between states are made, apply and end. It also describes peremptory international law.
44968.m: Ius cogens is defined in the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties.

44969.q: Which two elements are needed for customary international law to arise?
a: General practice and a belief that it is law
44969.e: Article 38(1)(b) of the ICJ Statute describes custom as evidence of a general practice accepted as law. So it needs state practice (consuetudo) and a belief that it is legally required (opinio iuris).
44969.m: Customary law arises from state practice and a belief that it is law.

44970.q: How does customary international law differ from a treaty?
a: It is not signed but grows out of the practice of states
It is issued by the UN Security Council
44970.e: A treaty is negotiated and signed. Customary law, by contrast, arises when states behave in the same way over a long time and feel legally bound in doing so.
44970.m: Customary law arises from how states behave, not from a signature.

44971.q: Which court decides disputes between states and applies treaties and customary international law?
44971.e: The International Court of Justice in The Hague relies on treaties, customary law and general principles of law. Court decisions and legal writings serve as aids.
44971.m: The International Court of Justice also applies customary international law.

44972.q: When is a state not bound by a new rule of customary international law?
a: If it has consistently objected to it from the start
If it has ignored it once
If it is not in the UN
If its parliament has not agreed
44972.e: A state that clearly and constantly objects to an emerging customary rule is not bound by it. This exception does not apply to peremptory rules such as the ban on torture.
44972.m: A state that objects early and consistently can avoid being bound by a new customary rule.

44973.q: According to the International Court of Justice, what is needed for a rule to become customary international law?
a: A widespread and uniform practice of states
The approval of the UN Secretary-General
A majority decision of the General Assembly
The signature of every state in the world
44973.e: In the North Sea cases of 1969, the ICJ required a widespread and uniform practice, backed by the belief that it is legally binding.
44973.m: Customary law needs widespread, uniform state practice.

44974.q: What was the name of the court in The Hague that settled disputes between states in the days of the League of Nations?
44974.e: The Permanent Court of International Justice worked from 1922. After the Second World War, the UN's International Court of Justice took its place.
44974.m: The Permanent Court of International Justice was the forerunner of the ICJ.

44975.q: What is meant by diplomatic asylum?
a: Protection for persecuted people in an embassy
44975.e: With diplomatic asylum, an embassy takes in a persecuted person. There are regional rules on this in Latin America, but it is not generally recognised worldwide.
44975.m: Diplomatic asylum is protection in an embassy.

44976.q: What is the task of the UN International Law Commission?
a: It writes down international law and develops it further
44976.e: The International Law Commission drafts treaties and summarises customary law. In 2018, for example, it set out how customary law can be identified.
44976.m: The International Law Commission codifies and develops international law.

44977.q: What does the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties regulate?
a: How states conclude, interpret and end treaties
The protection of prisoners of war
44977.e: The Convention is often called the “treaty on treaties”. It came into force in 1980. The rights of diplomats are governed by another Vienna Convention of 1961.
44977.m: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties is the “treaty on treaties”.

44978.q: What does the principle “pacta sunt servanda” mean?
a: The stronger party decides the treaty
44978.e: The principle is in Article 26 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties: every valid treaty binds the parties and must be carried out in good faith.
44978.m: Treaties must be kept in good faith.

44979.q: May a state end a treaty because circumstances have changed fundamentally?
a: Only exceptionally and under strict conditions
Yes, at any time without giving reasons
44979.e: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties allows a fundamental change of circumstances to be invoked only exceptionally. For boundary treaties it is ruled out completely.
44979.m: A fundamental change of circumstances can end a treaty only exceptionally.

44980.q: What are international treaties interpreted by first and foremost?
a: By their wording in context and by their object and purpose
By the will of the stronger state
By the law of the state that keeps the treaty
44980.e: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties requires interpretation in good faith, according to the ordinary meaning of the terms in their context and in the light of object and purpose. The preparatory work is only a supplementary means.
44980.m: Treaties are interpreted by wording, context, and object and purpose.

44981.q: May a state justify breaking a treaty with its own national law?
a: No, national law does not excuse a breach of treaty
Yes, national law always comes first
44981.e: Under the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, a state may not use its internal law as a reason for not carrying out a treaty. This also applies to constitutional law, with one narrow exception.
44981.m: National law does not excuse a breach of treaty.

44982.q: Which people may represent their state when concluding a treaty without full powers?
a: Head of state, head of government and foreign minister
44982.e: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties names heads of state, heads of government and foreign ministers, who by virtue of their office do not need to present full powers. Other people generally need them.
44982.m: Head of state, head of government and foreign minister need no full powers.

44983.q: What is a one-sided statement called with which a state wants to exclude the legal effect of certain treaty provisions for itself?
44983.e: Reservations are dealt with in Articles 19 to 23 of the Vienna Convention. They are not allowed, among other things, if they are incompatible with the treaty's object and purpose.
44983.m: With a reservation, a state limits how far it is bound by a treaty.

44984.q: What applies to a treaty that was forced on a state by the threat or use of force?
a: It is valid but can be terminated
It is valid for only five years
It must be confirmed by the Security Council
44984.e: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties declares void any treaty brought about by force in violation of the UN Charter. The rule is linked to the ban on the use of force.
44984.m: A treaty obtained by force is void.

44985.q: What duty does a state have that has signed a treaty but not yet ratified it?
a: It must not defeat the treaty's object and purpose
It must apply all provisions at once
It must ratify within a year
It has no duties at all
44985.e: A signatory state must not do things that would defeat the treaty's object and purpose. This applies until it makes clear that it does not intend to become a party.
44985.m: A state that signs must not undermine the treaty in advance.

44986.q: What does state immunity mean in international law?
a: A state cannot simply be sued in the courts of another state
A state may never be attacked
Heads of state may never be arrested
A state pays no customs duties
44986.e: States are equal in rank. So no state should sit in judgement over another sovereign state. Immunity from foreign courts follows from this.
44986.m: A state does not judge another state of equal rank.

44987.q: For which acts does a state usually enjoy immunity before foreign courts?
a: For sovereign acts such as legislation or military operations
For buying goods from private firms
For rental contracts with private individuals
For the business of its state railway
44987.e: Today most states distinguish between sovereign and commercial acts. Immunity applies only to sovereign acts.
44987.m: States enjoy immunity for sovereign acts.

44988.q: For which type of acts do most states no longer grant immunity today?
44988.e: If a state buys goods like a private person, for example, it acts iure gestionis. Under the restrictive theory that prevails today, it can be sued for this before foreign courts.
44988.m: A state that acts like a trader is treated like a trader.

44989.q: Which organisation in Strasbourg drew up the European Convention on State Immunity in 1972?
44989.e: The Convention was drawn up by the Council of Europe and signed in Basel in 1972. It follows the rule that states enjoy immunity only for sovereign acts.
44989.m: The European Convention on State Immunity comes from the Council of Europe.

44990.q: Which case on immunity in claims over Second World War crimes did the ICJ decide in 2012?
44990.e: Italian courts had ruled against Germany over war crimes committed by the Wehrmacht. The ICJ decided that Italy had violated Germany's state immunity, even in the case of serious violations of international law.
44990.m: According to the ICJ, state immunity applies even to claims over war crimes.

44991.q: A foreign state buys goods in Switzerland like a private company and does not pay. What applies according to today's view?
a: It can be sued in a Swiss court
Only the UN Security Council can decide
Only the International Court of Justice is competent
44991.e: If a state acts like a private party, it enjoys no immunity. Swiss courts also require the deal to have a sufficient link to Switzerland.
44991.m: A state that acts like a trader can be sued like a trader.

44992.q: What is the immunity called that prevents the seizure of state assets such as central bank reserves?
44992.e: Even if a state loses a case, its assets used for sovereign purposes usually may not be seized. This immunity from enforcement is broader than immunity from the court proceedings themselves.
44992.m: Immunity from enforcement protects state assets used for sovereign purposes from seizure.

44993.q: Why is the 2004 UN Convention on State Immunity not yet in force (as of 2025)?
a: Too few states have ratified it
The Security Council blocked it with a veto
The International Court of Justice declared it invalid
It only applies from the year 2050
44993.e: The UN General Assembly adopted the Convention in 2004. However, it needs 30 ratifications, and this number has not yet been reached.
44993.m: A convention only comes into force once enough states have ratified it.

44994.q: In which document was the right of peoples to self-determination named as an aim as early as 1945?
44994.e: Article 1 of the UN Charter names as an aim friendly relations based on equal rights and self-determination of peoples.
44994.m: The UN Charter already names the self-determination of peoples.

44995.q: How did the right of peoples to self-determination become binding treaty law in 1966?
a: It was included in the two UN human rights covenants
It was written into the NATO Treaty
The International Court of Justice declared it law
The General Assembly chose it as its theme of the year
44995.e: The Civil and Political Covenant and the Economic, Social and Cultural Covenant both begin in Article 1 with the sentence that all peoples have the right of self-determination.
44995.m: Both UN human rights covenants of 1966 begin with the right to self-determination.

44996.q: Which US President made the right to self-determination well known in 1918 with his Fourteen Points?
44996.e: In January 1918 Woodrow Wilson presented a peace programme that foresaw reorganising Europe along national lines. Lenin also promoted self-determination.
44996.m: Wilson's Fourteen Points made self-determination popular in 1918.

44997.q: Which development did the UN General Assembly promote in 1960 with its declaration on self-determination?
a: The building of the Berlin Wall
The enlargement of the Security Council
44997.e: Resolution 1514 called for a swift end to colonial rule. In 1960 alone, 17 states in Africa became independent.
44997.m: In 1960 the UN backed the independence of the colonies.

44998.q: What is the form of self-determination called that is achieved within an existing state, for example through autonomy?
44998.e: Internal self-determination means a say and autonomy within a state. External self-determination means choosing an international status, up to independence.
44998.m: Self-determination can also be achieved within a state.

44999.q: What conclusion did the ICJ reach in its 2010 advisory opinion on Kosovo?
a: The declaration of independence did not violate international law
Kosovo must remain part of Serbia
Kosovo is a member of the UN
44999.e: The ICJ answered only the narrow question of whether the 2008 declaration was contrary to international law, and said no. It did not comment on a general right to secession.
44999.m: In 2010 the ICJ found no breach of international law in Kosovo's declaration of independence.

45000.q: Which borders did most African states take over after independence?
a: The borders of the colonial era
The borders of the old kingdoms
Borders newly set by the UN
45000.e: Under the principle of uti possidetis, new states kept the colonial administrative borders to avoid border wars. That is why many peoples today live spread across several states.
45000.m: New states mostly took over the borders of the colonial era.

45001.q: Which Swiss example shows a population's self-determination within the federal state through votes?
a: The founding of the canton of Jura
The introduction of women's right to vote
45001.e: After several votes in the 1970s, the northern Jura districts separated from Bern. The canton of Jura has existed since 1979.
45001.m: The canton of Jura was created through votes in 1979.

45002.q: In which document is the general ban on the use of force between states laid down?
a: In the Charter of the United Nations
45002.e: Article 2(4) of the UN Charter bans the threat or use of force against other states. The Geneva Conventions, by contrast, govern how one must behave in war.
45002.m: The ban on the use of force is in the UN Charter.

45003.q: Under Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, what else is forbidden besides the use of force?
45003.e: The Charter already forbids the threat of force, for example an ultimatum threatening war. According to the prevailing view, economic pressure does not fall under the ban on the use of force.

45004.q: Which 1928 treaty outlawed war as a tool of national policy?
45004.e: The Kellogg-Briand Pact banned wars of aggression but contained no sanctions. It was a forerunner of the broader ban on force in the UN Charter.
45004.m: The Kellogg-Briand Pact outlawed war in 1928.

45005.q: Which two exceptions to the ban on the use of force does the UN Charter expressly provide?
a: Self-defence and authorisation by the Security Council
45005.e: Force is allowed only in self-defence under Article 51 or with Security Council authorisation under Chapter VII. Humanitarian intervention without a mandate is disputed.
45005.m: The Charter allows force only in self-defence or with a Security Council mandate.

45006.q: Which act counts as an act of aggression in international law?
a: An invasion of a country by foreign troops
A critical speech at the UN
45006.e: A 1974 resolution of the UN General Assembly gives examples of aggression, such as invasion, bombardment or blockading ports. Economic or diplomatic pressure is not included.
45006.m: An invasion is the classic example of aggression.

45007.q: What does it mean that the ban on the use of force also counts as customary law?
a: It applies to all states, even without a treaty
It applies only if a state agrees
45007.e: Customary law arises from the general practice of states and their belief that they are legally bound. In 1986 the International Court of Justice confirmed that the ban on force applies in this way alongside the Charter.
45007.m: According to the ICJ, the ban on force is also customary law.

45008.q: What is military action in a state at the request of its government called?
45008.e: If a lawful government invites foreign troops, the prevailing view is that the ban on force is not violated. This is disputed in the case of a civil war.
45008.m: With the government's consent, an intervention usually does not violate the ban on force.

45009.q: Which court has been able to prosecute individuals for a war of aggression (the crime of aggression) since 2018?
a: The European Court of Human Rights
The Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne
The Court of Justice of the EU
45009.e: The states parties to the Rome Statute agreed on a definition in Kampala in 2010. Since 2018 the International Criminal Court in The Hague has been able to prosecute this crime.
45009.m: The International Criminal Court can prosecute the crime of aggression.

45010.q: Why is a “humanitarian intervention” without a UN Security Council mandate disputed under international law?
a: It is not provided for as an exception in the UN Charter
It is allowed only for Switzerland
It is expressly allowed in Article 51
45010.e: The Charter recognises only self-defence and Security Council authorisation as exceptions. One example in the debate is NATO's operation in Kosovo in 1999.
45010.m: Humanitarian interventions without a UN mandate are legally disputed.

45011.q: Which condition does Article 51 of the UN Charter name for the right of self-defence?
45011.e: Article 51 speaks of the case of an armed attack. According to the ICJ, lesser uses of force do not justify armed self-defence.

45012.q: Until when may a state exercise self-defence under Article 51 of the UN Charter?
a: Until the Security Council has taken the necessary measures
Until the end of the calendar year
Indefinitely, even after the war ends
45012.e: The right of self-defence comes second to collective security. It lasts until the Security Council has taken the measures needed to maintain world peace.
45012.m: Self-defence applies until the Security Council acts.

45013.q: What duty does a state have under Article 51 of the UN Charter when it defends itself?
a: It must report to the Security Council immediately
It must go to the ICJ
It must warn the attacker beforehand
45013.e: Self-defence measures must be reported to the Security Council immediately. The ICJ treated a missing report as a sign against a genuine case of self-defence.
45013.m: Self-defence must be reported to the Security Council.

45014.q: What does the UN Charter generally forbid, with self-defence as an exception?
45014.e: Article 2 of the Charter forbids force and the threat of force between states. Exceptions are self-defence and measures decided by the Security Council.
45014.m: The Charter forbids force between states, except in self-defence.

45015.q: Which two limits from customary law also apply to any act of self-defence?
45015.e: Article 51 does not mention these limits explicitly, but the ICJ confirmed them as customary law. The response must not go beyond what is needed to fend off the attack.
45015.m: Self-defence must be necessary and proportionate.

45016.q: What does collective self-defence mean in international law?
a: Other states help an attacked state at its request
A state defends only its own territory
45016.e: A third state may only help if the attacked state asks it to. The International Court of Justice stated this in 1986 in the case Nicaragua v. United States.
45016.m: Collective self-defence needs a request for help from the victim.

45017.q: When did NATO first invoke Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty?
a: During the Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962
After the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989
45017.e: Article 5 is linked to the right of collective self-defence under Article 51 of the UN Charter. On 12 September 2001 the North Atlantic Council invoked it for the first time.
45017.m: NATO's Article 5 was first invoked after 11 September 2001.

45018.q: What is the disputed defence against a danger that is only possible and not yet imminent called?
45018.e: Pre-emptive self-defence against an imminent attack is accepted by many. Preventive force against a merely possible future danger is mostly regarded as unlawful.
45018.m: Preventive self-defence against merely possible dangers is mostly unlawful.

45019.q: What does the principle of distinction in international humanitarian law require?
a: Attacks may be directed only at military targets
Each side must wear its own uniforms
Prisoners must be separated by nationality
45019.e: The parties to a conflict must always distinguish between civilians and combatants and between civilian objects and military targets. This is set out in Article 48 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions.
45019.m: Attacks may only hit military targets.

45020.q: What did the ICJ call the principle of distinction in its 1996 nuclear weapons advisory opinion?
a: A cardinal principle of international humanitarian law
45020.e: The ICJ called the protection of civilians through distinction one of the cardinal principles. Weapons that cannot distinguish are forbidden.
45020.m: The principle of distinction is a cardinal principle of the law of war.

45021.q: Under Article 50 of Additional Protocol I, how must a person be treated in case of doubt?
45021.e: If there is doubt whether a person is a civilian, they count as a civilian. Likewise, an object normally used for civilian purposes is not to be treated as a military target in case of doubt (Article 52(3)).
45021.m: In case of doubt, a person counts as a civilian.

45022.q: What are indiscriminate attacks under Article 51 of Additional Protocol I?
a: Attacks that can hit military targets and civilians without distinction
Attacks without a declaration of war
45022.e: Forbidden are, for example, attacks that are not directed at a specific military target or that use means which cannot be aimed precisely. Area bombing of cities also falls under this.

45023.q: Under the principle of proportionality, when is an attack forbidden?
a: When the civilian harm is excessive compared with the expected military advantage
When it lasts more than a day
When it takes place without air support
45023.e: Article 51(5)(b) of Additional Protocol I forbids attacks where the expected civilian losses are out of proportion to the concrete and direct military advantage. This adds to the principle of distinction.
45023.m: Civilian harm must not be excessive.

45024.q: Under Article 43 of Additional Protocol I, who is in principle a combatant?
a: A member of the armed forces of a party to the conflict
Any armed person in the war zone
45024.e: Combatants are members of the armed forces, except medical and religious personnel. They may take a direct part in hostilities and get prisoner-of-war status if captured.
45024.m: Combatants are members of the armed forces of a party to the conflict.

45025.q: Which 1949 treaties form the core of international humanitarian law?
45025.e: The four Geneva Conventions of 1949 protect the wounded, prisoners of war and civilians. The Additional Protocols of 1977 contain, among other things, the principle of distinction.
45025.m: The Geneva Conventions are the core of international humanitarian law.

45026.q: Under Article 51(3) of Additional Protocol I, when does a civilian lose protection from attack?
a: For as long as they take a direct part in hostilities
As soon as they wear a uniform jacket
If they live in the border area
If they pay taxes to the enemy
45026.e: Civilians are protected unless and for as long as they take a direct part in hostilities. After that they regain protection.
45026.m: Civilians lose protection only while directly taking part in fighting.

45027.q: What is forbidden under Article 51(7) of Additional Protocol I?
a: Using civilians as shields for military targets
45027.e: Parties to a conflict may not use the presence of civilians to shield military targets from attack. However, a violation does not cancel the other side's duties towards those civilians.

45028.q: Under Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions, what must states check when introducing new weapons?
a: Whether their use would be forbidden by international law
Whether they are cheaper than old weapons
Whether they were made in their own country
45028.e: When developing, acquiring or introducing new weapons, states must check whether their use would be forbidden. Switzerland carries out its own legal reviews for this.
45028.m: New weapons must be legally reviewed under Additional Protocol I.

45029.q: Which conflicts does Additional Protocol II deal with?
45029.e: Additional Protocol II extends common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions for civil wars. It applies when armed groups under responsible command control parts of the territory.
45029.m: Additional Protocol II protects victims in civil wars.

45030.q: Which conflicts does Additional Protocol I treat like wars between states?
a: Struggles of peoples against colonial rule and racist regimes
45030.e: This means conflicts in which peoples, exercising their right to self-determination, fight against colonial rule, foreign occupation and racist regimes. This rule was one reason why some states did not ratify the Protocol.
45030.m: Additional Protocol I treats wars of liberation like international conflicts.

45031.q: Which protective emblem did Additional Protocol III of 2005 introduce?
45031.e: The Red Crystal is a red square standing on its point, free of any religious or national meaning. It has equal standing with the Red Cross and the Red Crescent.
45031.m: The third Additional Protocol introduced the Red Crystal.

45032.q: Which state is the depositary of the Geneva Conventions and their Additional Protocols?
45032.e: The Swiss Federal Council keeps the documents and receives ratifications. Switzerland ratified Additional Protocols I and II in 1982.
45032.m: Switzerland keeps the Geneva Conventions and their Additional Protocols.

45033.q: Which installations does Additional Protocol I specially protect because an attack could release dangerous forces?
a: Dams, dykes and nuclear power stations
45033.e: If dams, dykes or nuclear power stations are attacked, heavy losses among civilians can result. They are therefore specially protected and can be marked with three orange circles.
45033.m: Dams, dykes and nuclear power stations are under special protection.

45034.q: What is the task of the International Humanitarian Fact-Finding Commission, based in Bern?
a: Investigating serious violations of the law of war
45034.e: The Commission was formed in 1991 on the basis of Additional Protocol I. It establishes facts about alleged serious violations but does not convict anyone.
45034.m: The Humanitarian Fact-Finding Commission in Bern investigates serious violations of the law of war.

45035.q: Under Additional Protocol I, below what age may children not be recruited into armed forces?
45035.e: Additional Protocol I obliges the parties not to let children under 15 take part in hostilities and not to recruit them. A protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child later raised this protection.
45035.m: Under Additional Protocol I, children under 15 may not be recruited.

45036.q: According to the Ottawa Convention's definition, what sets off an anti-personnel mine?
a: The presence, proximity or contact of a person
Only the weight of a tank
45036.e: Article 2 defines an anti-personnel mine as a mine designed to be exploded by the presence, proximity or contact of a person. Mines designed for vehicles are not included.
45036.m: An anti-personnel mine is set off by a person.

45037.q: In which year was the Ottawa Convention signed?
45037.e: The Convention was opened for signature in Ottawa in December 1997 and came into force on 1 March 1999. Switzerland was one of the early states parties.
45037.m: The Ottawa Convention was signed in 1997.

45038.q: Which organisation received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1997 together with Jody Williams?
a: International Committee of the Red Cross
45038.e: The campaign (ICBL) and its coordinator Jody Williams were honoured for their work for the ban on mines. The cooperation between civil society and states is known as the Ottawa Process.
45038.m: The landmine campaign received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1997.

45039.q: What must states parties to the Ottawa Convention do with their stockpiled anti-personnel mines?
a: Give them to the UN for safekeeping
45039.e: Stockpiled mines must be destroyed no later than four years after the Convention enters into force for the state. For mined areas the deadline is ten years.
45039.m: Stockpiles of anti-personnel mines must be destroyed.

45040.q: When does withdrawal from the Ottawa Convention take effect if the state is involved in a war at the time?
a: Only after the conflict has ended
45040.e: Normally a withdrawal takes effect six months after it is announced. If the state is then involved in an armed conflict, it takes effect only after the conflict ends.
45040.m: You cannot leave the Ottawa Convention in the middle of a war.

45041.q: Which states announced their withdrawal from the Ottawa Convention in 2025, pointing to the threat from Russia?
a: The Baltic states, Poland and Finland
45041.e: Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and Finland justified the step with the changed security situation. The withdrawals took effect at the end of 2025 and the start of 2026.
45041.m: Several of Russia's neighbours left the Ottawa Convention in 2025.

45042.q: Which of these states is not a party to the Ottawa Convention (as of 2025)?
45042.e: Big military powers such as the USA, Russia and China have not joined the Convention. Canada hosted the signing conference.
45042.m: The USA, Russia and China are not parties to the Ottawa Convention.

45043.q: In which city is the Implementation Support Unit of the Ottawa Convention based?
45043.e: The Implementation Support Unit is hosted by the Geneva International Centre for Humanitarian Demining (GICHD). Switzerland supports this centre.
45043.m: The Ottawa Convention is supported from Geneva.

a: Munitions that scatter many small explosives over an area
Munitions that produce smoke for camouflage
45044.e: Cluster munitions release many explosive submunitions, each weighing less than 20 kilograms. They hit large areas at once.
45044.m: Cluster munitions scatter many small explosives over a large area.

45045.q: When did the Convention on Cluster Munitions come into force?
45045.e: After the 30th ratification, the Convention came into force on 1 August 2010. Switzerland ratified it in 2012.
45045.m: The ban on cluster munitions has applied since 2010.

45046.q: Which state started the negotiating process for the ban on cluster munitions in 2007?
45046.e: Norway invited countries to a conference in Oslo in February 2007, after the use of cluster munitions in Lebanon in 2006 had caused strong criticism. The process took place outside the UN weapons convention.
45046.m: Norway started the Oslo Process in 2007.

45047.q: Why are cluster munitions considered especially dangerous for civilians?
a: Many submunitions fail to explode and act like mines
They are visible only at night
45047.e: Cluster munitions scatter many small explosives over large areas. Duds often lie around for decades and later kill or injure civilians, often children.
45047.m: Cluster munition duds endanger civilians long after the war.

45048.q: What must states parties to the Convention on Cluster Munitions do with their stocks?
a: Destroy them within a fixed deadline
45048.e: Stockpiles must be destroyed no later than eight years after the Convention enters into force for the state. Contaminated areas must be cleared within ten years.
45048.m: Cluster munition stocks must be destroyed within a deadline.

45049.q: Which country is regarded as the most heavily contaminated by cluster munitions in the world?
45049.e: During the Vietnam War the USA dropped huge amounts of cluster bombs over Laos. Duds are still being cleared there today.
45049.m: Laos is the country most heavily contaminated by cluster munitions.

45050.q: Which state was the first to withdraw from the Convention on Cluster Munitions?
45050.e: Lithuania justified its withdrawal with the security situation after Russia's attack on Ukraine. The withdrawal took effect in March 2025.
45050.m: In 2025 Lithuania became the first state to leave the cluster munitions ban.

45051.q: Besides the ban, what does the Convention on Cluster Munitions especially oblige affected states to do?
45051.e: The Convention obliges affected states to provide medical care, rehabilitation and social inclusion for victims. It is seen as a model for victim assistance in disarmament law.
45051.m: The cluster munitions ban requires help for the victims.

45052.q: What do the 1907 Hague Regulations on land warfare govern?
a: The laws and customs of war on land
The rights of refugees in peacetime
45052.e: The Regulations are the annex to the Fourth Hague Convention of 1907. They lay down how armies must behave in war, for example towards prisoners and civilians.
45052.m: The Hague Regulations govern conduct in war on land.

45053.q: Which ruler suggested the first Hague Peace Conference of 1899?
45053.e: The Russian Tsar Nicholas II invited states to a conference on disarmament and peace in 1898. It took place in The Hague in 1899.
45053.m: The 1899 Hague Peace Conference goes back to Tsar Nicholas II.

45054.q: Which principle of the Hague Regulations forms the basis for later bans on weapons?
a: Parties to a war may not use every means
Prisoners must be freed at once
45054.e: The Regulations state that those at war do not have an unlimited right to choose their means. Later bans, for example on poison gas, are based on this.
45054.m: In war, not every means is allowed.

45055.q: According to the Hague Convention, what applies if there is no explicit rule for a situation in war?
a: The laws of humanity still apply
45055.e: The so-called Martens Clause of 1899 refers to the laws of humanity and the dictates of public conscience. It was later taken over into the Geneva Conventions.
45055.m: Even without an explicit rule, humanity applies in war.

45056.q: Under the Hague Regulations, when is a territory considered occupied?
a: When the hostile army actually controls it
When the enemy claims it on a map
When a plane has flown over it
45056.e: What matters is actual control. The occupation extends only to areas where this authority has been established and can be exercised.
45056.m: Occupation requires actual control over a territory.

45057.q: What do the Hague Regulations expressly forbid in occupied territories?
45057.e: The Regulations say briefly: pillage is formally forbidden. They also protect private property in occupied territories.
45057.m: Pillage is forbidden under the Hague Regulations.

45058.q: Under the Hague Regulations, what must militias wear, among other things, to count as belligerents?
a: A fixed sign recognisable at a distance
A flag with a white cross
45058.e: They need a commander responsible for them, a fixed distinctive sign, to carry arms openly and to obey the laws of war. This is so that fighters can be told apart from civilians.
45058.m: Fighters must make themselves recognisable with a sign.

45059.q: Which court stated in 1946 that the rules of the Hague Regulations had become customary international law?
a: International Court of Justice in The Hague
European Court of Justice in Luxembourg
45059.e: The Nuremberg Tribunal stated that by 1939 the rules of the Hague Regulations were recognised by all civilised nations. So they also applied to states that were not parties.
45059.m: Since the Nuremberg judgment, the Hague Regulations count as customary law.

45060.q: Under the Hague Regulations, what may armies not attack or bombard?
45060.e: Undefended towns, villages, dwellings and buildings are protected. The rule is an early expression of the protection of civilians.
45060.m: Undefended places must not be attacked.

45061.q: Which four powers formed the International Military Tribunal in Nuremberg?
45061.e: The four victorious powers in Europe each provided two judges (a main judge and a deputy) and their own prosecution teams.
45061.m: In Nuremberg the four victorious powers jointly judged the major war criminals.

45062.q: In which year did the Nuremberg trial of the major war criminals begin?
45062.e: The trial opened on 20 November 1945 in courtroom 600 of the Nuremberg Palace of Justice.
45062.m: The trial of the major war criminals began in November 1945.

45063.q: Which verdicts did the court reach in the main Nuremberg trial?
a: Death sentences, prison terms and acquittals
45063.e: Twelve defendants were sentenced to death, several received prison terms and three were acquitted. This shows that the court examined each case individually.
45063.m: Nuremberg produced death sentences, prison terms and acquittals.

45064.q: How did Hermann Göring escape the carrying out of his death sentence?
a: Suicide with cyanide in his cell
Death from heart failure before the verdict
45064.e: Göring took a poison capsule the night before the executions in October 1946. How he got it into his cell has still not been fully explained.
45064.m: Göring killed himself shortly before his execution.

45065.q: What was new about the Nuremberg trial of the major war criminals?
a: Leading politicians of a state stood personally before an international court
A war was officially ended for the first time
A court ruled on borders for the first time
Soldiers were decorated for the first time
45065.e: Until then states had been held responsible, not individuals. In Nuremberg, senior figures of the Nazi regime had to answer personally before a court of the victorious powers.
45065.m: In Nuremberg, state leaders were charged personally at international level for the first time.

45066.q: Which principle was laid down in the Nuremberg Principles?
a: Acting on orders does not free you from punishment
Heads of state enjoy full immunity
Only states, not people, can be punished
45066.e: Anyone who commits a crime under international law on orders remains responsible; the order can at most reduce the sentence. High officials can also be punished.
45066.m: An order does not excuse a crime under international law.

45067.q: Which rules did the 1947 Nuremberg Code lay down after the Doctors' Trial?
a: Ethical rules for experiments on humans
Rules for treating prisoners of war
Rules for the denazification of doctors
45067.e: In the Doctors' Trial, physicians were convicted for cruel human experiments in concentration camps. The Code requires, among other things, the voluntary, informed consent of the test subject.
45067.m: The Nuremberg Code requires voluntary consent for experiments on humans.

45068.q: Which charge came before an international court for the first time in Nuremberg?
45068.e: The London Charter named crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity. The last term covered, for example, the persecution and murder of the Jews.
45068.m: In Nuremberg, crimes against humanity were charged for the first time.

45069.q: What was the official name of the court in the Tokyo trials?
a: International Military Tribunal for the Far East
Allied War Court for the Pacific
United Nations Military Tribunal for Asia
45069.e: The International Military Tribunal for the Far East sat in Tokyo from 1946 to 1948. It was the Asian counterpart to Nuremberg.
45069.m: The Tokyo trials took place before the Military Tribunal for the Far East.

45070.q: Which Japanese Prime Minister at the time of the attack on Pearl Harbor was sentenced to death in Tokyo?
45070.e: General Hideki Tōjō was Prime Minister from 1941 to 1944. He was executed in Sugamo Prison in December 1948.
45070.m: Hideki Tōjō was the best-known person convicted in the Tokyo trials.

45071.q: Which central figure in Japan was not charged in the Tokyo trials, on the USA's decision?
45071.e: The American occupation authority wanted to use the Emperor as a support for a calm occupation. That is why he went unpunished and stayed on the throne.
45071.m: Emperor Hirohito was never put on trial.

45072.q: How many defendants were sentenced to death in the Tokyo trials?
45072.e: Seven defendants were hanged, among them a single civilian, the former Prime Minister Kōki Hirota. Most of the others received life imprisonment.
45072.m: Seven death sentences were handed down in Tokyo.

45073.q: Which criticism was often made of the Tokyo trials, as of the Nuremberg trials?
a: Sentences too mild for all defendants
45073.e: Critics said that only the losers were charged and that some charges were based on retroactive law. The Indian judge Radhabinod Pal therefore called for all defendants to be acquitted.
45073.m: The Tokyo trials were criticised as victors' justice.

45074.q: Who issued the charter of the court for the Tokyo trials in January 1946?
45074.e: MacArthur was Supreme Commander of the Allied occupation of Japan. Unlike in Nuremberg, the court was not based on a treaty between several states but on his decree.
45074.m: The Tokyo charter came from the head of the occupation, MacArthur.

45075.q: Which massacre in China was an important charge in the Tokyo trials?
45075.e: At the end of 1937 Japanese troops killed large numbers of civilians and prisoners of war in Nanking. General Iwane Matsui was held responsible and executed.
45075.m: The Nanking Massacre was tried in Tokyo.

45076.q: Which category did the main defendants in the Tokyo trials belong to?
45076.e: Class A concerned the planning and waging of the war of aggression by the state leadership. Classes B and C covered conventional war crimes and were tried before other courts in Asia.
45076.m: Class A war criminals were tried in Tokyo.

45077.q: Who set up the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in 1993?
45077.e: The Security Council created the court with Resolution 827, based on Chapter VII of the UN Charter. It was the first international criminal court since Nuremberg and Tokyo.
45077.m: The UN Security Council founded the Yugoslavia tribunal.

45078.q: In which city was the Yugoslavia tribunal based?
45078.e: The tribunal worked in The Hague in the Netherlands. The International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court are also based there.
45078.m: The Yugoslavia tribunal sat in The Hague.

45079.q: Which former Serbian President died in custody in 2006, before the Yugoslavia tribunal could reach a verdict?
45079.e: Milošević was the first former head of state before an international criminal court. He died in his cell in The Hague in March 2006, and his trial ended without a verdict.
45079.m: Slobodan Milošević died in custody in 2006 before the verdict.

45080.q: What was the Yugoslavia tribunal responsible for?
a: Serious crimes in the Yugoslav wars from 1991
Border disputes between the successor states
Crimes in Yugoslavia during the Second World War
Economic disputes after Yugoslavia broke up
45080.e: The tribunal prosecuted genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes on the territory of the former Yugoslavia since 1991. The first trial concerned Duško Tadić.
45080.m: The Yugoslavia tribunal prosecuted crimes from the wars from 1991 onwards.

45081.q: How did Radovan Karadžić live before he was arrested in Belgrade in 2008?
a: As a bearded healer under a false name
As a monk in a monastery in Greece
As a building worker under a false name in Vienna
As a shepherd in the mountains of Montenegro
45081.e: The former President of the Bosnian Serbs posed as the alternative healer “Dragan Dabić”. He was later sentenced to life imprisonment.
45081.m: Karadžić hid for years as a healer in Belgrade.

45082.q: In which year did the Yugoslavia tribunal complete its work?
45082.e: The tribunal was dissolved at the end of December 2017. Its remaining tasks were taken over by a UN successor body.
45082.m: The Yugoslavia tribunal closed at the end of 2017.

45083.q: Against whom could the Yugoslavia tribunal bring charges?
a: Against individuals, including heads of state
Only against organisations such as armies
45083.e: International criminal courts prosecute individuals, not states. Soldiers were charged as well as generals and presidents.
45083.m: International criminal courts charge people, not states.

45084.q: Which court is now permanently responsible for genocide and war crimes, unlike the time-limited tribunals for Yugoslavia and Rwanda?
a: The European Court of Human Rights
45084.e: The International Criminal Court in The Hague has worked since 2002 on the basis of the Rome Statute. The International Court of Justice, by contrast, decides disputes between states.
45084.m: The International Criminal Court is a permanent criminal court.

45085.q: In which city was the Rwanda tribunal based?
45085.e: The tribunal sat in Arusha in Tanzania, outside Rwanda. There the safety of witnesses and defendants could be better ensured.
45085.m: The Rwanda tribunal sat in Arusha in Tanzania.

45086.q: Which crime of 1994 was the UN's Rwanda tribunal mainly responsible for?
45086.e: In 1994 hundreds of thousands of people, mainly Tutsi, were killed in Rwanda within a few months. The UN Security Council created the tribunal with Resolution 955.
45086.m: The Rwanda tribunal prosecuted the 1994 genocide.

45087.q: Roughly how many people were killed in the 1994 genocide in Rwanda?
45087.e: In only about 100 days between April and July 1994, an estimated 800,000 to one million people were killed.
45087.m: Almost a million people died in the genocide in Rwanda.

45088.q: What was special about the 1998 verdict against Jean-Paul Akayesu?
a: First verdict by an international court for genocide
First acquittal by any international court
First verdict for a war of aggression since 1946
First death sentence by a UN tribunal
45088.e: For the first time, an international court applied the 1948 Genocide Convention in a verdict. Akayesu was sentenced to life imprisonment.
45088.m: Akayesu was the first person convicted of genocide by an international court.

45089.q: In which country was the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda based?
45089.e: The Rwanda tribunal sat in Arusha in Tanzania, outside Rwanda. This was so that the proceedings could be carried out safely and independently.
45089.m: The Rwanda tribunal was based in Arusha in Tanzania.

45090.q: Against which population group was the 1994 genocide in Rwanda mainly directed?
45090.e: In 1994 extremist Hutu murdered mainly Tutsi, but also moderate Hutu. The Rwanda tribunal prosecuted those mainly responsible.
45090.m: The genocide in Rwanda was directed mainly against the Tutsi.

45091.q: Which radio station was at the centre of the Rwanda tribunal's “Media Trial”?
a: Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines
45091.e: The station RTLM stirred up hatred against Tutsi and called for murders. In 2003 the tribunal convicted leading media figures of incitement to genocide.
45091.m: Hate messages on the radio can be incitement to genocide.

45092.q: Whom was the Rwanda tribunal mainly meant to bring to trial?
a: Those mainly responsible for the genocide
45092.e: The UN tribunal dealt with leaders from politics, the army and the media. The many other cases were handled in Rwanda by courts and the Gacaca village courts.
45092.m: The Rwanda tribunal prosecuted those mainly responsible for the genocide.

45093.q: In which year was the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court adopted?
45093.e: A diplomatic conference in Rome adopted the Statute on 17 July. This day is now marked as the Day of International Criminal Justice.
45093.m: The Rome Statute was adopted in Rome in 1998.

45094.q: Can the International Criminal Court prosecute crimes from the Second World War?
a: No, only acts from its start in 2002
Yes, but only with UN approval
45094.e: The Rome Statute came into force on 1 July 2002. The Court cannot prosecute acts from before then; there used to be separate tribunals for that, as in Nuremberg.
45094.m: The Criminal Court judges only acts from 2002 onwards.

45095.q: What does the principle of complementarity mean for the International Criminal Court?
a: It steps in only if states do not prosecute themselves
It replaces all national criminal courts
It judges only states, not people
It needs the UN Security Council for every case
45095.e: States are responsible first. The Court acts only if a state is unwilling or unable to investigate genuinely.
45095.m: The Criminal Court complements national justice; it does not replace it.

45096.q: Is Switzerland a state party to the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court?
a: No, it has only signed it
45096.e: Switzerland deposited its instrument of ratification on 12 October 2001, making it one of the first states parties.
45096.m: Switzerland has been a state party to the Rome Statute since 2001.

45097.q: What was the Congolese militia leader Thomas Lubanga convicted of in 2012, in the International Criminal Court's first verdict?
45097.e: Lubanga had conscripted children into his militia in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and made them fight. He received 14 years in prison.
45097.m: The Criminal Court's first verdict concerned child soldiers.

45098.q: Which of these states has not joined the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court?
45098.e: In Rome in 1998, 120 states voted in favour and 7 against, including the USA and China. Russia and India are not states parties today either.
45098.m: The USA, China and Russia do not belong to the Criminal Court.

45099.q: Against which serving head of state did the International Criminal Court issue an arrest warrant in 2009 for crimes in Darfur?
45099.e: The Sudanese President was wanted for crimes against humanity and war crimes, and later also for genocide. He nevertheless travelled to several countries without being arrested.
45099.m: There was an international arrest warrant against Sudan's President al-Bashir.

45100.q: Why did the International Criminal Court issue an arrest warrant against Vladimir Putin in 2023?
45100.e: The warrant concerns the abduction of children from occupied areas of Ukraine to Russia. It also applies to Russia's children's rights commissioner.
45100.m: The arrest warrant against Putin concerns the abduction of children.

45101.q: What does the principle of universal jurisdiction in criminal law say?
a: Any state may prosecute serious crimes under international law
A state prosecutes only acts on its own territory
A state prosecutes only acts by its own citizens
A state prosecutes only acts against its own citizens
45101.e: For crimes such as genocide or torture, it does not matter where they were committed or what nationality the perpetrators and victims have. The other answers describe the principle of territoriality and the principles of nationality.
45101.m: Under universal jurisdiction, the gravest crimes may be prosecuted anywhere.

45102.q: Which country issued the warrant on which Augusto Pinochet was arrested in London in 1998?
45102.e: The Spanish investigating judge Baltasar Garzón requested extradition for torture and murder. But Pinochet was allowed to return to Chile for health reasons.
45102.m: The Pinochet case made universal jurisdiction known worldwide.

45103.q: In which country was the world's first verdict on state torture in Syria reached in 2022?
45103.e: The Higher Regional Court in Koblenz sentenced a former Syrian intelligence officer to life imprisonment. It based its ruling on universal jurisdiction.
45103.m: State torture in Syria was punished for the first time in Germany.

45104.q: Which court convicted the former Liberian rebel commander Alieu Kosiah of war crimes in 2021?
a: The Federal Criminal Court in Bellinzona
The Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne
45104.e: Kosiah was arrested in Switzerland and sentenced to 20 years in prison. It was the first war crimes trial before a civilian federal court in Switzerland.
45104.m: Switzerland also prosecutes war crimes committed abroad.

45105.q: What did the Federal Criminal Court convict a former minister from the Gambia of in 2024?
45105.e: Ousman Sonko was interior minister under Yahya Jammeh and was sentenced to 20 years at first instance. The acts took place in the Gambia; he was prosecuted under universal jurisdiction.
45105.m: A former Gambian minister stood trial in Bellinzona.

45106.q: In which country was the former President of Chad, Hissène Habré, sentenced to life imprisonment in 2016?
45106.e: Extraordinary African Chambers in Dakar convicted him of torture, war crimes and crimes against humanity. For the first time, a court of one state judged the former head of state of another state.
45106.m: Habré was convicted by an African court in Dakar.

45107.q: In which city did the trial of Adolf Eichmann take place in 1961?
45107.e: The Israeli secret service had kidnapped Eichmann in Argentina in 1960. Israel also relied on universal jurisdiction, as the acts had been committed before the state was founded.
45107.m: Eichmann was put on trial in Jerusalem.

45108.q: Which condition does the Swiss Criminal Code require for crimes under international law with no link to Switzerland to be prosecuted there?
a: The act was committed in Europe
45108.e: Under Article 264m of the Criminal Code, the person must be in Switzerland and must not be handed over to another state or an international court.
45108.m: Switzerland prosecutes crimes under international law if the offender is in the country.

45109.q: When was the Srebrenica massacre committed?
45109.e: On 11 July 1995 Bosnian Serb troops took the enclave. In the following days the men and boys were killed.
45109.m: The Srebrenica massacre happened in July 1995.

45110.q: How many Bosniak men and boys were murdered in Srebrenica?
45110.e: More than 8,000 victims were killed and buried in mass graves. Many were later identified by DNA analysis.
45110.m: More than 8,000 people were murdered in Srebrenica.

45111.q: Soldiers from which country were meant to protect the UN safe area of Srebrenica?
45111.e: A lightly armed Dutch blue helmet battalion was stationed in the enclave. It could not prevent the attack; Dutch courts later held the state partly responsible.
45111.m: Dutch blue helmets could not protect Srebrenica.

45112.q: What did the International Court of Justice find in 2007 in the case Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia?
a: Serbia failed to prevent the genocide
There was no genocide in Srebrenica
Bosnia shares the blame for the massacre
45112.e: The Court confirmed that genocide took place in Srebrenica. Serbia was not found to be the perpetrator but had breached its duty to prevent it and to hand over the perpetrators.
45112.m: Serbia breached its duty to prevent the genocide.

45113.q: Which international court was the first to classify the Srebrenica massacre as genocide?
a: The European Court of Human Rights
45113.e: In 2001 the Yugoslavia tribunal convicted General Radislav Krstić and stated that genocide took place in Srebrenica. The International Court of Justice confirmed this in 2007.
45113.m: The Yugoslavia tribunal classified Srebrenica as genocide in 2001.

45114.q: In which present-day country is Srebrenica?
45114.e: Srebrenica is in eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina, near the border with Serbia. The memorial to the victims is in Potočari near Srebrenica.
45114.m: Srebrenica is in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

45115.q: Which day did the UN General Assembly declare in 2024 as the international day of remembrance of the Srebrenica genocide?
45115.e: The day of remembrance falls on the day the enclave fell. Serbia and Republika Srpska rejected the resolution.
45115.m: Srebrenica is remembered worldwide on 11 July.

45116.q: Which Bosnian Serb army chief was sentenced to life imprisonment, partly for Srebrenica?
45116.e: Mladić was in hiding for years and was arrested in Serbia in 2011. The life sentence was upheld on appeal in 2021.
45116.m: Ratko Mladić was convicted as commander for Srebrenica.

45117.q: In which year was Slobodan Milošević handed over to the Yugoslavia tribunal?
45117.e: After his fall from power he was arrested in Belgrade and taken to The Hague on 28 June 2001.
45117.m: Milošević was handed over to the tribunal in 2001.

45118.q: What was new in 1999 about the indictment against Slobodan Milošević?
a: A serving head of state was charged for the first time
Someone was convicted in absentia for the first time
A war of aggression was charged for the first time
NATO charged a person for the first time
45118.e: Milošević was President of Yugoslavia when the tribunal charged him for crimes in Kosovo. No international court had ever charged a serving head of state before.
45118.m: Milošević was charged while serving as head of state.

45119.q: How did the trial of Slobodan Milošević end?
a: He died in custody before the verdict
He was sentenced to life imprisonment
He was acquitted on all counts
It was dropped because of immunity
45119.e: Milošević died of a heart attack in his cell in March 2006. Because no verdict was reached, he is not legally regarded as convicted.
45119.m: The trial of Milošević ended without a verdict.

45120.q: How did Slobodan Milošević defend himself before the tribunal?
a: With a team of US lawyers
He stayed silent throughout the trial
Through a court-appointed lawyer from Serbia
45120.e: Milošević rejected the court as illegitimate and mostly conducted his defence in person. This made the trial much longer.
45120.m: Milošević used the trial as a stage for his own defence.

45121.q: Which conflicts did the indictment against Slobodan Milošević cover?
a: Kosovo, Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina
Bosnia and Herzegovina, Slovenia and Hungary
45121.e: The three indictments were joined into one trial. For Bosnia, the charges also included genocide.
45121.m: Milošević was charged over three wars in the former Yugoslavia.

45122.q: Who handed Slobodan Milošević over to the tribunal in The Hague in 2001?
a: The police of Bosnia and Herzegovina
45122.e: Prime Minister Zoran Đinđić pushed the handover through, partly because Western reconstruction aid depended on it. He was murdered in Belgrade in 2003.
45122.m: Serbia itself handed Milošević over to The Hague.

45123.q: Which offices did Slobodan Milošević hold one after the other?
a: President of Serbia, then of Yugoslavia
President of Bosnia, then of Serbia
Army chief, then President of Montenegro
Head of government of Croatia, then of Serbia
45123.e: He was President of Serbia from 1989 to 1997 and then President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia until his fall in 2000.
45123.m: Milošević ruled first Serbia and then Yugoslavia.

45124.q: How did the Special Court for Sierra Leone come into being?
a: Through an agreement between the UN and Sierra Leone
Through a resolution of the African Union
As a chamber of the International Criminal Court
As a military court of the government
45124.e: The Court was a mixed court with local and international judges, based in Freetown. It relied on international law and on the law of Sierra Leone.
45124.m: The Special Court for Sierra Leone was a mixed court.

45125.q: Charles Taylor, who was convicted by the Special Court for Sierra Leone, was President of which country?
45125.e: Taylor supplied the rebels in the neighbouring country with weapons. He was the first former head of state since Nuremberg to be convicted by an international court.
45125.m: Charles Taylor was President of Liberia.

45126.q: What was the former Liberian President Charles Taylor convicted of in 2012?
a: Aiding and abetting war crimes in Sierra Leone
45126.e: Taylor supplied the rebels in Sierra Leone with weapons and received diamonds in return. The court sentenced him to 50 years in prison.
45126.m: Charles Taylor was convicted for crimes in Sierra Leone.

45127.q: Why did the trial of Charles Taylor take place in The Hague rather than in Sierra Leone?
a: There were fears of unrest in West Africa
Sierra Leone had no court building
Taylor was allowed to choose the place himself
He faced the death penalty in Sierra Leone
45127.e: For security reasons, the Special Court held this trial in The Hague. After the verdict Taylor was sent to a prison in the UK.
45127.m: The Taylor trial was moved to The Hague for security reasons.

45128.q: What was the rebel group RUF notorious for in Sierra Leone's civil war?
45128.e: The Revolutionary United Front under Foday Sankoh terrorised the population and also used child soldiers. Sankoh died before his trial ended.
45128.m: The RUF committed serious crimes against civilians in the civil war.

45129.q: With which raw material did the rebels in Sierra Leone mainly finance their war?
45129.e: The rebels controlled diamond fields and sold the stones via Liberia. This gave rise to the term “blood diamonds”.
45129.m: Blood diamonds financed the civil war in Sierra Leone.

45130.q: Which act did the Special Court for Sierra Leone recognise in 2008 for the first time as a crime against humanity?
45130.e: Women and girls were abducted by fighters and made into “wives”. The Appeals Chamber treated this as another inhumane act.
45130.m: Forced marriage can be a crime against humanity.

45131.q: In which years did the Khmer Rouge rule Cambodia?
45131.e: The Khmer Rouge took Phnom Penh in April 1975. At the start of 1979 they were overthrown by Vietnamese troops.
45131.m: The Khmer Rouge ruled for about four years.

45132.q: Roughly how many people died under Khmer Rouge rule?
45132.e: Executions, forced labour, hunger and disease killed about a fifth to a quarter of the population.
45132.m: About a quarter of Cambodians died under the Khmer Rouge.

45133.q: What was Tuol Sleng in Phnom Penh under Khmer Rouge rule?
45133.e: In prison S-21, in a former school, thousands of prisoners were interrogated and killed. Its head, Duch, was the first to be convicted by the Khmer Rouge tribunal; today the site is a memorial.
45133.m: Tuol Sleng was the most notorious Khmer Rouge prison.

45134.q: How was the Khmer Rouge tribunal made up?
a: Judges of the International Criminal Court
45134.e: The Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia were based on an agreement with the UN. Verdicts needed a majority that included at least one international judge.
45134.m: The Khmer Rouge tribunal was a mixed court.

45135.q: Why did Pol Pot never stand before the Khmer Rouge tribunal?
a: He died in 1998, before it was set up
He fled to China and stayed there
He was pardoned by the government
He had immunity as head of state
45135.e: The Khmer Rouge leader died in 1998 in the jungle on the border with Thailand. The tribunal only began its work in 2006.
45135.m: Pol Pot was never convicted for his crimes.

45136.q: What were the leading Khmer Rouge figures Nuon Chea and Khieu Samphan convicted of in 2018, among other things?
a: A war of aggression against Thailand
45136.e: The tribunal convicted both of genocide against the Vietnamese minority, Nuon Chea also against the Muslim Cham, and of crimes against humanity. Both received life imprisonment.
45136.m: The Khmer Rouge tribunal found that genocide had taken place.

45137.q: In which city was the Khmer Rouge tribunal based?
45137.e: The tribunal sat on the outskirts of the Cambodian capital; it completed its trials in 2022. This allowed many survivors to follow the proceedings themselves.
45137.m: The Khmer Rouge tribunal sat in Phnom Penh.

45138.q: What is meant by the crime of aggression in international criminal law?
a: Planning and waging an unlawful war of aggression
Insulting a foreign head of state
45138.e: The definition was added to the Rome Statute as Article 8bis at the Kampala conference in 2010. It means an attack that manifestly violates the UN Charter.
45138.m: Aggression means an unlawful war of aggression.

45139.q: Since which year has the International Criminal Court been able to prosecute the crime of aggression?
45139.e: The states parties decided at the end of 2017 to activate jurisdiction; it has applied since 17 July 2018.
45139.m: Jurisdiction over aggression has only applied since 2018.

45140.q: Under the Rome Statute, who can commit the crime of aggression?
a: Only those who actually direct the state's leadership
Any soldier fighting at the border
Only the attacking state as a whole
45140.e: Aggression is a leadership crime: only someone who effectively controls the political or military action of a state can commit it.
45140.m: Only the top leaders of a state are liable for aggression.

45141.q: Under what name was planning a war of aggression charged in Nuremberg?
a: Breach of the League of Nations
45141.e: The judgment called the war of aggression the “supreme international crime”, because it contains within itself all the other evils.
45141.m: In Nuremberg, aggression was called crimes against peace.

45142.q: Under Article 8bis, what threshold must an act of aggression reach to count as the crime of aggression?
a: A manifest violation of the UN Charter by its character, gravity and scale
At least a thousand civilian deaths
A duration of more than a year
45142.e: Not every border incident is enough. By its character, gravity and scale, the act of aggression must amount to a manifest violation of the Charter.
45142.m: Only manifest violations of the UN Charter count as the crime of aggression.

45143.q: Under the umbrella of which organisation is the special tribunal for the crime of aggression against Ukraine, agreed in 2025, being set up?
45143.e: President Zelensky and Secretary General Alain Berset, a former Swiss Federal Councillor, signed the agreement in Strasbourg in June 2025. The International Criminal Court cannot prosecute aggression by citizens of non-member states.
45143.m: A Council of Europe special tribunal is to punish the aggression against Ukraine.

45144.q: Which state was the first to ratify the Kampala amendments on the crime of aggression in 2012?
45144.e: Liechtenstein had strongly shaped the negotiations; its UN ambassador Christian Wenaweser chaired the Assembly of States Parties.
45144.m: Liechtenstein was the first state to ratify the Kampala amendments.

45145.q: Under the Rome Statute, what condition makes an act a crime against humanity?
a: Being part of a widespread or systematic attack on civilians
Being committed during an international armed conflict
Intending to destroy an ethnic group completely
At least a thousand victims in one state
45145.e: Article 7 requires a widespread or systematic attack against a civilian population, and the offender must know about it.
45145.m: Crimes against humanity are part of an attack on the civilian population.

45146.q: Which condition applied in Nuremberg to crimes against humanity but is no longer required today?
a: An order from the state leadership
45146.e: The Nuremberg Charter linked these crimes to the war. Today they can also be committed in peacetime.
45146.m: Crimes against humanity also exist in peacetime.

45147.q: In connection with which events did France, the UK and Russia first speak of crimes “against humanity” in 1915?
a: The crushing of the Boxer Rebellion
The poison gas attacks at Ypres
45147.e: The Entente warned the Ottoman government that it would hold those responsible personally to account. The term later entered international law.
45147.m: The term crimes against humanity dates from 1915.

45148.q: In which trials after the Second World War were crimes against humanity first charged before an international court?
45148.e: The 1945 Charter of the Nuremberg Military Tribunal named crimes against humanity as a separate charge for the first time. The international lawyer Hersch Lauterpacht shaped the idea of protecting the individual person.
45148.m: Crimes against humanity were first charged in Nuremberg.

45149.q: Which element does genocide require, but a crime against humanity does not?
a: The intent to destroy a protected group
An attack on the civilian population
45149.e: Genocide requires the special intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group as such.
45149.m: Genocide requires an intent to destroy a group.

45150.q: Which system of oppression does the Rome Statute expressly list as a crime against humanity?
45150.e: Apartheid means an institutionalised regime of systematic oppression of one racial group by another. The term comes from South Africa.
45150.m: Apartheid is a crime against humanity.

45151.q: For how long can crimes against humanity be prosecuted in Switzerland?
45151.e: Article 101 of the Criminal Code states that genocide, crimes against humanity and serious war crimes are not subject to any limitation period.
45151.m: In Switzerland, the gravest crimes under international law never become time-barred.

45152.q: What is the crime called in which the state arrests people and conceals their fate or whereabouts?
45152.e: The victims are removed from the protection of the law, and their relatives learn nothing. This practice became known, for example, under military dictatorships in Latin America.
45152.m: Enforced disappearance is a crime against humanity.

45153.q: What does international humanitarian law mean by forbidden perfidy?
a: Attacking by abusing trust in protection
Any deception of the enemy through camouflage
An attack at night without warning
45153.e: It is forbidden, for example, to pretend to be a civilian or a wounded person, or to misuse the Red Cross, in order to attack. Ordinary ruses of war such as camouflage remain allowed.
45153.m: Ruses of war are allowed; perfidy is forbidden.

45154.q: Which method of warfare does the Rome Statute expressly name as a war crime?
45154.e: It is forbidden to deliberately deprive the civilian population of things essential for survival, such as food, or to obstruct relief supplies.
45154.m: Starving the civilian population is a war crime.

45155.q: Under the Rome Statute, recruiting children below what age into armed forces is a war crime?
45155.e: The Statute forbids conscripting children under 15 or using them to take an active part in fighting. Many states campaign for a limit of 18.
45155.m: Using child soldiers under 15 is a war crime.

46357.q: What do you call an autocracy in which a group of senior officers rules together?
46357.e: The Spanish word ‘junta’ means assembly or committee. Examples are the military governments in Argentina from 1976 to 1983 and in Greece from 1967 to 1974.
46357.m: A military junta is a government made up of several senior officers.

46358.q: What do you call a regime in which elections are held regularly but are neither free nor fair?
46358.e: In an electoral autocracy there are elections, but the opposition and media are suppressed. Research projects such as V-Dem distinguish it from closed autocracies without elections.
46358.m: Electoral autocracies hold elections that are neither free nor fair.

46359.q: Which title of the Russian tsars expressed the claim to unlimited sole rule?
46359.e: The Russian title ‘Samoderzhets’ means autocrat, literally ‘self-ruler’. It stressed that the tsar's power did not come from a constitution or a parliament.
46359.m: The Russian tsars called themselves autocrats, claiming unlimited power.

46360.q: Which feature fundamentally distinguishes an autocracy from a democracy?
a: The lack of checks on power by the people
46360.e: Autocracies also have armies, taxes and capitals. What matters is that the government cannot be checked and removed through free elections, separation of powers and independent courts.
46360.m: Autocracies above all lack effective control of power by the people.

46361.q: In research, what do you call a dictatorship in which power is centred entirely on one individual?
46361.e: The political scientist Barbara Geddes distinguished military regimes, one-party regimes and personalist regimes. In personalist regimes everything depends on the ruler and their inner circle.
46361.m: In personalist regimes power is concentrated in one person.

46362.q: What does political science mean by ‘autocratisation’?
a: The introduction of a planned economy
46362.e: Autocratisation means a process in which free elections, media freedom or the separation of powers are gradually weakened. It can happen in democracies as well as in states that are already authoritarian.
46362.m: Autocratisation is the gradual erosion of a state's democratic features.

46363.q: In research, what do you call states that mix features of democracy and autocracy?
46363.e: Hybrid regimes combine, for example, regular elections with restricted press freedom and a dependent judiciary. They lie in a grey zone between democracy and closed autocracy.
46363.m: Hybrid regimes lie in a grey zone between democracy and autocracy.

46364.q: Which feature did Juan Linz name for authoritarian regimes as opposed to totalitarian ones?
46364.e: According to Linz, authoritarian regimes allow a limited, unaccountable pluralism, for example the Church, the army or business associations. Totalitarian regimes, by contrast, tolerate no independent centres of power.
46364.m: Authoritarian regimes tolerate limited pluralism, totalitarian ones do not.

46365.q: Which values do authoritarian regimes often invoke instead of spreading a closed ideology?
a: Human rights and separation of powers
46365.e: The political scientist Juan Linz called such basic attitudes ‘mentalities’. They are more flexible than an ideology such as communism and do not demand total conviction from the population.
46365.m: Authoritarian regimes appeal to values such as order and nation rather than to a closed ideology.

46366.q: Using which regime as an example did Juan Linz develop his concept of the authoritarian regime in 1964?
46366.e: In 1964 Linz published the study ‘An Authoritarian Regime: Spain’. For him the Franco regime was neither a democracy nor a totalitarian system.
46366.m: Franco's Spain served Juan Linz as the model case of an authoritarian regime.

46367.q: Which authoritarian regime ended on 25 April 1974 with the Carnation Revolution?
46367.e: The Estado Novo built up by António de Oliveira Salazar was overthrown in 1974 by a largely bloodless military coup. Soldiers put carnations in the barrels of their rifles.
46367.m: The Carnation Revolution of 1974 ended Portugal's Estado Novo.
